t: Laxative mechanisms: bulk-forming holds water and expands stool; osmotic draws water into the lumen; stimulant activates enteric nerves; secretagogue increases chloride and fluid secretion → softer stool, faster transit.
**Loperamide — a peripheral opioid-receptor agonist that slows GI motility without significant CNS (opioid) effects at normal doses.**
Opioid brake on the gut: opioid agonist binds mu receptors on enteric neurons → less acetylcholine release → slower peristalsis, longer transit → more water absorbed, firmer stool.
Diphenoxylate/atropine — a combination opioid-receptor agonist; **atropine is included at a subtherapeutic dose specifically to discourage misuse/overdose**.
Bismuth subsalicylate — antisecretory, mild antimicrobial, and anti-inflammatory effects; also used for dyspepsia.
Opioid receptor antagonists (methylnaltrexone, naloxegol, naldemedine, alvimopan) block gut μ-receptors without entering the CNS, so analgesia is kept.
**PEG is first-line for chronic constipation**; magnesium laxatives need caution in CKD.

Onset (Figure 2, illustrative): osmotic ~2 h and stimulant ~8 h act fastest; secretagogue ~1 day; stool softener ~2 days and bulk-forming ~60 h take longest. **A patient who needs relief tonight is not a bulk-forming candidate.**
Stimulants cause cramping and are for short-term use. Lubiprostone causes nausea; linaclotide causes diarrhea.

t: **Mesalamine, sulfasalazine — anti-inflammatory action local to the GI mucosa.** Sulfasalazine reaches the colon → colonic bacteria cleave the azo bond → 5-ASA (mesalamine) plus sulfapyridine released → 5-ASA acts on mucosa, reducing inflammatory mediators → less mucosal inflammation.
Azathioprine is converted to 6-mercaptopurine → metabolized to thioguanine nucleotides → block purine synthesis in lymphocytes → fewer proliferating T and B cells → slow, sustained remission.

**Targeted therapy:** TNF-α inhibitors block tumor necrosis factor-alpha (infliximab, adalimumab); the integrin inhibitor blocks α4β7 integrin-mediated leukocyte gut-homing (vedolizumab); the IL-12/23 inhibitor blocks interleukin-12 and -23 signaling (ustekinumab); the JAK inhibitor blocks intracellular JAK signaling (tofacitinib).
Vedolizumab is the most **gut-selective** agent — less systemic immunosuppression than TNF inhibitors, JAK inhibitors, or thiopurines.
**Chemistry & formulations:** azo compounds (sulfasalazine, balsalazide, olsalazine) are cleaved by colonic bacteria; mesalamine formulations release 5-ASA at set pH or times.
5-ASA: first-line for mild-to-moderate ulcerative colitis; more limited role in Crohn disease.
Corticosteroids: short-term induction of remission during an acute flare; not appropriate for long-term maintenance given cumulative toxicity.
Immunomodulators: long-term maintenance of remission; onset is slow (weeks to months) — not useful for acute flares.
Delayed-release forms target the ileum or colon; enemas and suppositories treat distal disease.
Corticosteroids: prednisone 40–60 mg/d for flares, tapered after response; rectal forms for distal disease; not for maintenance.
**The major safety theme across immunomodulators and biologics: immunosuppression → increased infection risk.**

Why is vedolizumab gut-selective? α4β7 integrin is the gut-homing address tag; block it and leukocytes can’t enter the bowel, while immunity elsewhere is spared.

**What patients take on their own can change how their medications work.** Ask one question about any vitamin: can it build up to toxic levels?

**Fat-soluble (A, D, E, K):** stored in adipose tissue and the liver; accumulate with excess intake — real toxicity risk; absorption depends on dietary fat and bile, impaired by fat-malabsorption conditions.
**Water-soluble (B-complex, C):** not significantly stored — excreted renally; toxicity is rare except at very high supplemental doses; deficiency develops more quickly without ongoing intake.

Figure 8 (illustrative storage/toxicity-risk index): vitamin A 85 and D 90 (fat-soluble) vs. C 10 and B-complex 8 (water-soluble). Vitamin D and A toxicity from OTC overuse are the clearest real examples.
Cyanocobalamin (B12), folic acid, vitamin D, phytonadione (K1), ferrous sulfate.

t: **B12 absorption:** dietary B12 is bound to food protein → stomach acid and pepsin release it → free B12 binds intrinsic factor from parietal cells → the complex is absorbed in the terminal ileum.
Reduced vitamin K is recycled by VKORC1; **warfarin blocks VKORC1, so fewer active factors** — active vitamin K carboxylates clotting factors II, VII, IX, X — so fewer active factors.

**Two ways to lower warfarin’s effect:** dietary vitamin K opposes it pharmacodynamically (supports clotting factor synthesis); St. John’s wort induces CYP enzymes and speeds clearance — a pharmacokinetic interaction. **Result: lower INR and less anticoagulation.**
**Enteral nutrition** (oral or tube feeding) is preferred whenever the gut is functional — **“if the gut works, use it”**; lower infection/complication risk.

**Parenteral nutrition** is delivered intravenously, bypassing the GI tract entirely; reserved for a non-functional or inaccessible GI tract; requires close monitoring — electrolyte shifts, refeeding syndrome, catheter-related infection (the main parenteral risk).
Treat B12 deficiency with intramuscular or high-dose oral B12.
**Vitamin B12 deficiency:** megaloblastic anemia and neurologic symptoms/neuropathy that can become irreversible if treatment is delayed.

**Ginkgo biloba and fish oil — can increase bleeding risk, especially combined with anticoagulants/antiplatelets.**
**At risk for B12 deficiency:** long-term PPI or H2 blocker use, metformin (impairs ileal uptake), bariatric surgery, older age, vegan diets.
St. John’s wort activates PXR, inducing CYP 3A4, 2C9, 1A2 and P-glycoprotein: lowers digoxin, birth control, cyclosporine, HIV drugs, warfarin; serotonin syndrome with antidepressants.
Garlic, ginkgo and ginseng have antiplatelet effects — avoid or monitor with anticoagulants and around surgery.

Fat-soluble vitamin absorption depends on dietary fat and bile.
Monitor B12 in long-term PPI or metformin users.
**Keep vitamin K intake consistent rather than avoiding it.** Check INR when starting or stopping any supplement; stopping St. John’s wort can raise INR.
**Refeeding:** start feeding slowly in malnourished patients; check phosphate, potassium and magnesium daily at the start; give thiamine before feeding begins.
**Supplements are not held to the same FDA premarket efficacy/safety standards as prescription drugs — potency and purity can vary by product.**
Always ask patients specifically about supplement use — many don’t mention it unless asked; counsel them to disclose all supplement use to every prescriber and pharmacist.

Applying the whole GI & Nutrition toolkit: for each patient, name a first-line approach AND the single biggest safety concern to check before prescribing/counseling.
**1.** Acid-peptic disease and antiemetics are managed by targeting specific points along well-defined pathways (parietal cell secretion; the vomiting reflex).
**2.** PPIs are the most potent antisecretory agents, but long-term use carries real risks that warrant periodic reassessment.

**3.** IBD therapy follows a step-wise escalation matched to disease severity. **4.** Biologic agents share mechanisms and immunosuppression risk across organ systems. **5.** Nutrition and supplements are not inert.
Pharmacology is cumulative, not siloed by unit: biologic mechanisms (Lecture 2) and drug-metabolism/interaction concepts (Lecture 1) reappear here in a new organ system.
**Patient A — GERD symptoms, needs rapid occasional relief:** an antacid for occasional relief; an H2 blocker or PPI if frequent.
**Patient B — confirmed H. pylori, penicillin allergy:** bismuth quadruple therapy.
**Patient C — moderate-to-severe Crohn disease, inadequately controlled on azathioprine:** a biologic or small molecule such as an anti-TNF agent.
**Patient D — warfarin patient starting an herbal mood supplement:** counsel on St. John’s wort and check INR.
**Recall Q1:** PPIs block the H⁺/K⁺-ATPase proton pump itself — the final common pathway for gastrin, histamine, and acetylcholine — unlike H2RAs, which block only the histamine input.

Laxatives fall into four buckets — **bulk-forming** (slowest, safest), **osmotic** (fast; PEG first-line), **stimulant** (short-term), **secretagogue** (IBS-C) — and osmotic/stimulant act in hours, bulk-forming in days.
**Loperamide** and **diphenoxylate/atropine** slow the gut via mu receptors; never use them in **C. difficile** or bloody/febrile diarrhea, and atropine is there to deter misuse.
IBD therapy **steps up with severity**: 5-ASA → short-term steroids → thiopurines for maintenance (test TPMT/NUDT15; cut dose with allopurinol) → biologics/small molecules.
Biologics share **immunosuppression risk**: screen TB and hepatitis B/C and update vaccines first; **vedolizumab** is the gut-selective one.
**Fat-soluble** vitamins (A, D, E, K) accumulate; water-soluble are excreted. Long-term **PPI or metformin** → check **B12**; refeed slowly with thiamine.

Warfarin’s effect falls with **dietary vitamin K** (pharmacodynamic) and with **St. John’s wort** (CYP3A4 induction, pharmacokinetic); ginkgo and fish oil raise bleeding — always ask about supplements.
L07 · Endocrine Pharmacotherapy — Session 1 — study guide
**One regulatory template governs thyroid, adrenal, and gonadal control alike.**

**Figure 1. Original illustrative diagram (not from Katzung): the hypothalamus drives the anterior pituitary, which drives a target endocrine gland, whose peripheral hormone produces end-organ effects and negatively feeds back to suppress the levels above it.**
This is the conceptual spine for the unit — thyroid, adrenal and gonadal pharmacology all map onto this three-level axis; return to it every time a new gland appears.
The peripheral hormone negatively feeds back on the hypothalamus/pituitary above it — which explains why every exogenous hormone therapy in the unit suppresses the levels above it.
Somatropin (GH deficiency); octreotide, lanreotide, pegvisomant (GH excess); cabergoline, bromocriptine (prolactin); desmopressin (DI); tolvaptan, demeclocycline (SIADH).

t: GH axis (Figure 2): pituitary somatotroph releases GH → GH drives liver IGF-1 production → octreotide and lanreotide bind somatostatin receptors and lower GH release.
Pegvisomant blocks the GH receptor so IGF-1 falls → acromegaly symptoms improve (monitor IGF-1). GH rises on pegvisomant, so GH is not used to monitor it.

Dopamine normally inhibits prolactin release — dopamine agonists restore that inhibitory tone. Hypothalamic dopamine is the brake on lactotrophs; prolactinoma or drugs (antipsychotics, metoclopramide) lift the brake.
Cabergoline or bromocriptine activate D2 receptors → prolactin release falls and the tumor often shrinks → cycles and fertility return; galactorrhea resolves.
ADH (Figure 4): ADH binds the V2 receptor in the collecting duct → aquaporin-2 channels insert → water is reabsorbed and urine concentrates.
Desmopressin boosts this (diabetes insipidus); tolvaptan or demeclocycline blunt it (SIADH) → free water retained in DI therapy, excreted in SIADH therapy.
Anterior pituitary hormones & their hypothalamic regulators: continuous (not pulsatile) GnRH analogs down-regulate GnRH receptors and suppress LH and FSH.
**●  GH deficiency:** treated with recombinant human growth hormone (somatropin); monitor growth velocity in children and IGF-1 levels in adults.

**●  GH excess (acromegaly):** treated with somatostatin analogs (octreotide, lanreotide — suppress GH release), the GH-receptor antagonist pegvisomant, or dopamine agonists (cabergoline) in select cases.
**●  Clinical pearl:** octreotide also has major uses outside the pituitary axis — variceal bleeding and carcinoid syndrome — worth flagging as a cross-system agent.
**●  Indication:** octreotide and lanreotide treat acromegaly; octreotide also treats carcinoid syndrome and variceal bleeding.
Hyperprolactinemia: dopamine agonists are first-line — cabergoline, bromocriptine — used for prolactinomas and drug-induced hyperprolactinemia.

Diabetes insipidus (ADH deficiency/resistance): desmopressin (DDAVP) for central DI. SIADH (ADH excess): fluid restriction first-line; vasopressin-receptor antagonists (tolvaptan) or demeclocycline for refractory cases.
**●  Somatropin (GH deficiency):** monitor growth velocity or IGF-1.
**●  Adverse effects:** GI upset, gallstones and bradycardia with octreotide and lanreotide (also glucose changes).

Oxytocin (posterior pituitary) is given IV to start or augment labor; it also triggers milk letdown. Its half-life is about 5 minutes.

**A life-threatening hyperthyroid crisis requiring rapid, multi-pronged therapy.** Thyroid storm is treated with four drugs that hit four targets.

Beta-blockers (propranolol) — control adrenergic symptoms (tachycardia, tremor) and blunt peripheral T4-to-T3 conversion. PTU (preferred over methimazole) — blocks new hormone synthesis and peripheral conversion.

Iodine solution (given after PTU/methimazole) — acutely blocks hormone release; must follow the antithyroid drug to avoid providing substrate for new synthesis. Corticosteroids — blunt peripheral conversion and treat relative adrenal insufficiency.

Laboratory diagnosis of Graves disease: suppressed TSH with high free thyroid hormone. Management of Graves disease: antithyroid drugs, radioactive iodine, or thyroidectomy; methimazole preferred except in pregnancy and storm.
Pregnant hypothyroid patients often need about 25–30% more levothyroxine; add two extra doses a week as soon as pregnancy is confirmed.
Methimazole boxed warning: agranulocytosis, hepatotoxicity. PTU boxed warning: severe hepatotoxicity (more than methimazole) — reserve for specific indications.

**Glucocorticoid power and mineralocorticoid balance — and what happens when therapy stops.**

**Figure 9. Original illustrative diagram (not from Katzung): chronic exogenous glucocorticoid use suppresses CRH and ACTH via negative feedback, reducing endogenous cortisol production — abrupt withdrawal can precipitate adrenal insufficiency.**
This is the single most clinically important concept in the glucocorticoid section — it explains why tapering (not stopping) is the standard of care.
Prednisone, dexamethasone, hydrocortisone (glucocorticoids); fludrocortisone (mineralocorticoid); ketoconazole, metyrapone, mifepristone, spironolactone (antagonists).

t: Glucocorticoids (e.g., prednisone, dexamethasone): anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressive effects, with a spectrum of relative potency and mineralocorticoid activity across agents.

Signaling (Figure 8): prednisone or cortisol crosses the cell membrane → binds the cytoplasmic glucocorticoid receptor → the complex moves into the nucleus → switches on anti-inflammatory genes and represses NF-kB cytokines → fewer inflammatory cells and mediators.
Mineralocorticoids (fludrocortisone): promote renal sodium retention and potassium excretion.

Synthesis chain (Figure 10): cholesterol enters the adrenal cortex → CYP enzymes convert it to cortisol and aldosterone → ketoconazole blocks several enzymes; metyrapone blocks the last cortisol step (11-beta-hydroxylase).
Then cortisol or aldosterone binds its receptor → mifepristone blocks the glucocorticoid receptor; spironolactone blocks the mineralocorticoid receptor. Receptor blockers leave hormone levels high.
Glucocorticoids are used across nearly every organ system for inflammatory/autoimmune disease.

Fludrocortisone: replacement therapy in primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease), alongside a glucocorticoid — primary adrenal insufficiency needs BOTH hormone classes replaced, not just cortisol.
**●  Ketoconazole:** inhibits multiple steps in steroidogenesis (CYP enzymes); used for Cushing syndrome; significant drug-interaction and hepatotoxicity concerns.
**●  Metyrapone:** blocks the final step of cortisol synthesis (11-β-hydroxylase); used diagnostically and for Cushing syndrome.

**●  Mifepristone:** a glucocorticoid-receptor antagonist; used for hyperglycemia associated with Cushing syndrome when surgery is not an option (distinct from its progesterone-receptor antagonist use in pregnancy termination).

**●  Spironolactone:** a mineralocorticoid-receptor antagonist; used for hyperaldosteronism and as a potassium-sparing diuretic — ties back to the diuretic pharmacology concepts from earlier coursework.
Addison disease: hydrocortisone 20–30 mg daily (more during stress) plus fludrocortisone 0.05–0.2 mg/d.
Dexamethasone suppression test diagnoses Cushing syndrome; antenatal glucocorticoids reduce neonatal respiratory distress.
**●  Adverse effects:** hyperglycemia, osteoporosis, infection, mood change, cataracts, adrenal suppression.

Case: chronic high-dose prednisone for a rheumatologic condition, stopped abruptly after running out of refills; now hypotension, weakness, nausea, confusion. **What is the most likely cause of this presentation, and how should it be managed?**
**This presentation is consistent with acute adrenal insufficiency (adrenal crisis) from abrupt glucocorticoid withdrawal after HPA-axis suppression.**
**Management requires immediate IV hydrocortisone (which has both glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid activity) and IV fluids — this is a medical emergency, not a routine medication-refill issue.**
The fix for a missed refill here is not "just restart the pill" — it is emergent IV steroid replacement; tapering protects against it.

Mifepristone’s dual identity (glucocorticoid-receptor antagonist here vs. progesterone-receptor antagonist elsewhere) is worth flagging explicitly — don’t conflate the two uses or assume a single mechanism.

Drug names reveal the class: **-tide** somatostatin analog (octreotide, lanreotide; lowers GH release); **-pressin** vasopressin analog (desmopressin; central diabetes insipidus); **-vaptan** V2 antagonist (tolvaptan; SIADH).

**-ergoline** dopamine agonist, ergot-derived (cabergoline; lowers prolactin); **-thyroxine** thyroid hormone (levothyroxine; replacement, titrate to TSH); **-imazole / -thiouracil** thionamide antithyroid (methimazole, propylthiouracil; blocks hormone synthesis).

**-sone / -solone** corticosteroid (prednisone, dexamethasone; anti-inflammatory, taper); **-conazole** azole steroidogenesis inhibitor (ketoconazole; Cushing syndrome); **-pristone** receptor antagonist (mifepristone; glucocorticoid-receptor block); **-lactone** mineralocorticoid antagonist (spironolactone; hyperkalemia risk).
**A stem is a memory aid, not a rule: where no shared stem exists, learn the class name instead.**
Recap: **1.** The hypothalamic-pituitary-target gland axis (Figure 1) is a shared regulatory template across thyroid, adrenal, and gonadal systems — drug therapy can intervene at any level.

**2.** Thyroid hormone synthesis has distinct, drug-targetable steps (Figure 6); PTU uniquely blocks peripheral T4-to-T3 conversion, making it preferred in thyroid storm and first-trimester pregnancy.
**3.** Chronic exogenous glucocorticoid use suppresses the HPA axis (Figure 9) — abrupt withdrawal risks adrenal crisis, so chronic therapy is tapered, not stopped.

**4.** Adrenocortical antagonists (ketoconazole, metyrapone, mifepristone, spironolactone) block cortisol or aldosterone synthesis/action at different points for Cushing syndrome and hyperaldosteronism. **5.** Session 2 (Thursday, November 12) continues with gonadal hormones, diabetes, and parathyroid disorders.
Older synthesis inhibitors — aminoglutethimide and trilostane — and the adrenolytic mitotane are rarely used; mifepristone (RU-486) is the receptor antagonist.
Synthesis inhibitors & glucocorticoid antagonists: metyrapone is the only adrenal inhibitor usable in pregnancy; abiraterone treats refractory prostate cancer; mifepristone half-life about 20 hours.

**while hypoparathyroidism (deficient PTH, low calcium) is treated with calcitriol and oral calcium, sometimes with recombinant PTH 1-84 in severe cases.**
Figure 22 is the organizing concept for the section — two opposite pathologies, two opposite drug strategies, both targeting the same hormone axis.

t: Cinacalcet — a calcimimetic; activates the calcium-sensing receptor on parathyroid cells, reducing PTH secretion.
Chain (Figure 23): parathyroid cells sense calcium through the CaSR → low calcium keeps PTH release high → cinacalcet makes the receptor more sensitive to calcium.
The cell reads calcium as high and lowers PTH → PTH and serum calcium fall.
Calcitriol (active vitamin D) plus oral calcium — mainstay for hypoparathyroidism, since PTH deficiency impairs vitamin D activation; calcitriol bypasses the PTH activation step.
Cinacalcet: used for secondary hyperparathyroidism (e.g., in chronic kidney disease on dialysis) and parathyroid carcinoma.
Recombinant human PTH 1-84 — reserved for patients not adequately controlled on calcium/calcitriol alone.
Cinacalcet adverse effects: nausea, hypocalcemia and QT prolongation, so monitor calcium.

Opposite monitoring targets: watch for hypocalcemia with cinacalcet, hypercalcemia/hypercalciuria with calcitriol/PTH replacement — a symmetry worth drawing out.

Case: a patient with chronic kidney disease is found to have an elevated PTH level with low-normal serum calcium. A second, unrelated patient who underwent recent thyroidectomy develops perioral numbness and low serum calcium with a low PTH level.
**How does drug therapy differ between these two patients?**
**The CKD patient has secondary hyperparathyroidism and may benefit from cinacalcet to reduce PTH secretion.**

**The post-thyroidectomy patient has surgical hypoparathyroidism (inadvertent parathyroid gland injury) and needs calcitriol plus calcium replacement — the opposite pharmacologic strategy for the opposite underlying problem.**
Post-thyroidectomy hypoparathyroidism is a classic, testable scenario and a bridge back to thyroid surgery from Session 1 (antithyroid drugs can also precede surgical management).

**Applying the whole Endocrine pharmacology toolkit.** The shared principle is negative feedback suppression by exogenous hormone. For each patient, name a first-line approach AND the single biggest safety concern.

**1.** The hypothalamic-pituitary-target gland axis is a shared template across thyroid, adrenal, and gonadal pharmacology — exogenous hormone therapy suppresses the levels above it via negative feedback.
**2.** Antithyroid drug selection (methimazole vs. PTU) and glucocorticoid tapering both hinge on understanding exactly where and how each drug intervenes in its pathway.
**3.** Glucose-lowering drugs act at distinct sites (pancreas, liver, muscle/fat, kidney, gut, incretin axis) — drug selection balances efficacy against hypoglycemia and other class-specific risks.

**4.** Hyperparathyroidism and hypoparathyroidism require opposite drug strategies (lowering vs. raising effective PTH activity) — a new angle distinct from, but related to, the osteoporosis pharmacotherapy of Unit 2.
**5.** Endocrine pharmacology is deeply interconnected — spironolactone, dopamine agonists, and SERMs each reappear across more than one organ system in this unit alone.
Connecting back: osteoporosis pharmacology (Unit 2) and drug-metabolism/interaction concepts (Unit 1) both reappear here — pharmacology is cumulative, not siloed by unit.
**Patient A — Graves disease, in thyroid storm:** PTU (blocks synthesis and peripheral T4-to-T3 conversion); check liver toxicity.
**Patient B — chronic prednisone user, abruptly out of refills:** restart the glucocorticoid and taper; the risk is adrenal insufficiency from HPA suppression.
**Patient C — type 2 diabetes, older adult with fall history, needs add-on therapy:** DPP-4 or SGLT2 inhibitor; avoid sulfonylurea hypoglycemia.
**Patient D — post-thyroidectomy, perioral numbness and low calcium:** calcitriol plus calcium; monitor for hypercalcemia.

**Combined contraception** suppresses GnRH/FSH/LH; no estrogen with prior VTE/stroke, **smoker ≥ 35**, **migraine with aura**, estrogen-sensitive cancer, uncontrolled hypertension → progestin-only. Inducers (rifampin) need backup.
**Tamoxifen** blocks breast but activates endometrium (report bleeding); **raloxifene** activates bone, blocks endometrium; both raise VTE. **Finasteride** lowers DHT and halves PSA.
**Insulin**: rapid (lispro, aspart), short (regular — the only IV insulin), NPH, basal (glargine, detemir, degludec); main risk **hypoglycemia** (rule of 15; beta-blockers mask it).

**Metformin** first-line (avoid eGFR < 30, hold for contrast, B12); **sulfonylureas** highest oral hypoglycemia; **TZDs** fluid/heart failure; **SGLT2** genital infections, euglycemic DKA, cardiorenal benefit.
**GLP-1 RAs** (weight loss; no MTC/MEN2) and **DPP-4 inhibitors** (weight neutral) work glucose-dependently — low hypoglycemia; older adult who falls → DPP-4 or SGLT2.
**Hyperparathyroidism** → cinacalcet (watch hypocalcemia); **hypoparathyroidism** → calcitriol + calcium (watch hypercalcemia).
L09 · Renal Pharmacotherapeutics — Session 1 — study guide
**Where diuretics act, and why renal function changes how every drug is dosed.** Renal physiology and pharmacokinetic principles set the dosing logic for everything that follows.
**The kidney is a major route of elimination for many drugs and active metabolites — renal function directly determines how long a drug stays in the body.**
Glomerular filtration rate (GFR) and creatinine clearance (CrCl) are the standard measures used to estimate renal drug-elimination capacity.

This is foundational Chapter 3 content applied specifically to the renal unit: renal dosing is not a separate topic but the lens through which every drug in this unit (and this course) should be viewed.

Digoxin, most antibiotics (e.g., vancomycin, many beta-lactams), many direct oral anticoagulants, metformin, and the diuretics covered later in this session are examples of drugs requiring renal dose adjustment.

t: Flow (Figure 1): GFR falls → renally cleared drug or active metabolite accumulates → toxicity.

**Figure 2. Original illustrative diagram (not from Katzung): filtrate flows through the proximal tubule, thick ascending limb, distal convoluted tubule, and collecting duct — each diuretic class blocks sodium reabsorption at a different, specific segment.**
Share of filtered sodium reabsorbed: proximal tubule about 65%, thick ascending limb about 25%, distal tubule 5-8%, collecting duct 2-3% — this previews the potency ranking in Figure 7.
This nephron map is the conceptual spine of the session — every diuretic class is anchored back to its segment.
Match each diuretic class to the nephron segment where it acts: loop diuretics (furosemide) — thick ascending limb; thiazide diuretics (hydrochlorothiazide) — distal convoluted tubule.

Potassium-sparing — aldosterone antagonists (spironolactone) and ENaC blockers (amiloride) — collecting duct; carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (acetazolamide) — proximal tubule; osmotic diuretics (mannitol) — throughout.
CAI — proximal tubule; osmotic — acts osmotically throughout the filtrate-containing segments, mainly the proximal tubule and descending limb.
Renal tubule transport mechanisms: the proximal tubule reabsorbs about 66% of Na⁺ and 85% of NaHCO₃; organic acid secretion there delivers most diuretics to their luminal site.
Collecting tubule system: only 2–5% of NaCl, but where aldosterone acts and K⁺ is secreted; upstream diuretics deliver more Na⁺ here — the basis of diuretic K⁺ wasting.
Renal autacoids: adenosine (A1) lowers GFR; prostaglandins (PGE2) aid loop action; natriuretic peptides (nesiritide) and urodilatin cause natriuresis but have a limited clinical role.
Three levers: reduce the dose, extend the dosing interval, or both — the specific approach depends on the drug. Reduced GFR makes a renally cleared drug accumulate if unadjusted.
Reduce the maintenance dose when the drug’s effect is concentration-dependent; extend the dosing interval when the drug has a long half-life; monitor for toxicity after each dose change.
Loading doses are often unchanged; maintenance doses are what get adjusted.
As GFR falls, renally cleared drugs accumulate — dosing must be adjusted by reducing the dose, extending the interval, or both.

Pharmacokinetics in two numbers: volume of distribution links amount in the body to concentration; clearance links elimination rate to concentration.
Maintenance dose = clearance × target concentration (steady state depends only on clearance); loading dose = volume of distribution × target concentration, given slowly IV.
Drug accumulation: doses repeated more often than every four half-lives accumulate; steady state takes about four half-lives.
Check creatinine clearance before dosing any renally cleared drug (lower maintenance dose, extend the interval, or check CrCl) — especially in older adults.
Reassess as renal function changes — acute illness, dehydration, or new nephrotoxic drugs can drop GFR quickly.
When in doubt, consult dosing references or clinical pharmacy — this is not a "memorize every number" exercise; the point is the habit of checking renal function before dosing.
Distribution & clearance: adjust a renally cleared drug in proportion to creatinine clearance (Cockcroft-Gault; women 85% of the calculated value).
The target concentration strategy: choose a target, predict V and CL from weight and renal function, dose, measure the response, revise, repeat.
Dosing history: without it a drug level loses its predictive value; draw digoxin at least 6 hours after a dose.
Renal function determines drug dosing broadly, not just for diuretics — GFR/creatinine clearance should be checked before dosing any renally cleared drug (Chapter 3).
Textbook case: 85-year-old, 60 kg, CrCl 22 mL/min — digoxin clearance falls to 3.7 L/h, so about 127 mcg/day: two 62.5-mcg tablets.

Loops are the most potent class; thiazides are first-line for hypertension.

t: **Mechanism: block the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter (NKCC2) in the thick ascending limb — the site responsible for ~25% of filtered sodium reabsorption.**

**Figure 3. Original illustrative diagram (not from Katzung): loop diuretics block NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb, reducing Na+/Cl-/K+ reabsorption and collapsing the lumen-positive potential that normally drives paracellular calcium and magnesium reabsorption —**

**explaining the increased calcium and magnesium excretion seen with this class.** The lumen-positive potential (from K⁺ recycling) is the link students skip when they memorize “loops cause hypocalcemia” without the why.
**Mechanism: block the Na-Cl cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule — a less potent natriuretic site (~5–8% of filtered sodium) than the loop.**
Follow the thiazide chain step by step (Figure 4): NCC block in the DCT → sodium and water loss → lower intracellular sodium → calcium retained through the NCX exchanger → falling urinary calcium.
Contrast this with loop diuretics, which raise urinary calcium (Figure 3).

In one line: loop diuretics collapse the lumen-positive potential driving paracellular Ca²⁺/Mg²⁺ reabsorption (↑ excretion); thiazides increase distal calcium reabsorption through a separate mechanism (↓ excretion).
Loops work from the lumen, so their effect tracks proximal secretion; NSAIDs and probenecid compete and reduce it. NSAIDs also blunt the PGE2 contribution.
Loops: edema (heart failure, cirrhosis, renal disease) and, at times, hypertension when a thiazide alone is insufficient (e.g., significant renal impairment).
Loop diuretics increase calcium excretion — useful in hypercalcemia, and the opposite effect of thiazides.
Hydrochlorothiazide, chlorthalidone — first-line agents for essential hypertension; chlorthalidone has a longer half-life and is often preferred for 24-hour BP control.
Thiazides decrease calcium excretion — can be therapeutically useful in patients with osteoporosis and recurrent calcium-containing kidney stones.
Hypercalcemia: normal saline plus IV furosemide (80–120 mg) — a loop alone causes volume contraction and stops working.
Nephrolithiasis: thiazide plus more fluid and less salt; do not restrict dietary calcium.
Diabetes insipidus (nephrogenic, including lithium-induced): thiazides reduce polyuria; amiloride blocks lithium entry; monitor lithium levels.
Nonedematous states, hypertension: chlorthalidone lowers BP more than HCTZ but has more adverse effects; loops reserved for GFR < 30–40 mL/min or heart failure.
**Adverse effects: hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, metabolic alkalosis, ototoxicity (especially with rapid IV administration or high doses), and hyperuricemia.**

Case: hypertension and worsening CKD (eGFR now 25 mL/min), well controlled on chlorthalidone for years, but blood pressure has crept up. **What is the most likely explanation, and what change in therapy would you consider?**

**Thiazide diuretics lose much of their natriuretic efficacy once GFR falls below roughly 30 mL/min, because there is too little filtered sodium reaching the distal tubule for the drug to act on meaningfully.**
**A loop diuretic, which acts upstream at the thick ascending limb, remains effective even in advanced CKD and is the more appropriate choice here.**
The “thiazides lose efficacy in advanced CKD” point bridges directly to Session 2’s hypertension-in-CKD content.
Edematous states, heart failure: loops are standard, but overdiuresis cuts preload and cardiac output; hypokalemia worsens arrhythmias and digitalis toxicity.
Kidney disease and renal failure: little benefit below GFR 5 mL/min; high-dose loops or loop plus metolazone treat overload; avoid acetazolamide.
Textbook case: HCTZ added to chronic furosemide in CKD → 15 kg lost, BP 91/58, creatinine 10.8 — hypovolemic AKI; monitor closely, ideally inpatient.
Site, potency · Loop diuretics: Thick ascending limb — most potent natriuresis (~25%) · Thiazide diuretics: Distal convoluted tubule — modest natriuresis (~5–8%)

t: Aldosterone binds the mineralocorticoid receptor → increases ENaC and Na/K pump activity → K+ and H+ secreted into the tubule. Blocking either step reduces potassium and hydrogen secretion.
Spironolactone and eplerenone block the receptor (block aldosterone’s effect directly); amiloride and triamterene block ENaC directly, independent of aldosterone.
**Acetazolamide (carbonic anhydrase inhibitor):** blocks Na+/HCO3- reabsorption in the proximal tubule → less HCO3- reabsorbed → bicarbonate diuresis, metabolic acidosis; weak diuretic effect.
**Mannitol (osmotic diuretic):** an inert, filtered but poorly reabsorbed solute that holds water in the tubule lumen osmotically — osmotic diuresis.
Side by side: acetazolamide removes bicarbonate reabsorption; mannitol removes water reabsorption by staying in the lumen. Both act before the loop, so their natriuretic potency is modest.
Figure 6 (**Schematic (illustrative)**): proximal tubule — carbonic anhydrase inhibition and osmotic holding of water (illustrative schematic).

**Figure 7. Original illustrative comparison (illustrative values, not from Katzung): loop diuretics block roughly 25% of filtered sodium reabsorption, substantially more than thiazides, carbonic anhydrase inhibitors, or potassium-sparing diuretics —**
**directly reflecting the percentage normally reabsorbed at each nephron segment in Figure 2.** This is why loops are reached for first when potent natriuresis is the goal.
Potassium-sparing agents are often used in combination with a loop or thiazide diuretic specifically to offset potassium loss from the more potent class.
Acetazolamide: valued for non-diuretic uses — glaucoma (reduces aqueous humor production), altitude sickness prophylaxis, and metabolic alkalosis correction; also raised intracranial pressure.
Mannitol: used to reduce elevated intracranial or intraocular pressure and in certain cases of rhabdomyolysis-associated kidney injury prevention.
Know the niche, not an everyday use: acetazolamide = glaucoma/altitude sickness; mannitol = ICP/IOP reduction.
Potassium-sparing diuretics fit mineralocorticoid excess: primary (Conn syndrome) or secondary hyperaldosteronism (heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome).
Hepatic cirrhosis: resistant to loops but unusually responsive to spironolactone; aggressive diuresis risks hepatorenal syndrome and encephalopathy.
Renal & cardiac protection: aldosterone antagonists are cardioprotective and lower albuminuria; finerenone slowed CKD in type 2 diabetes.
Idiopathic edema (women 20–30): rule out surreptitious diuretic use; prefer moderate salt restriction.

**Primary adverse effect across the class: hyperkalemia — the risk rises sharply when combined with ACE inhibitors, ARBs, or in renal impairment (a direct preview of Session 2's cardiorenal drug-interaction content).**

Case: a patient with stage 3 chronic kidney disease and heart failure is taking an ACE inhibitor and is started on spironolactone for additional heart-failure benefit; two weeks later a routine basic metabolic panel shows potassium 6.1 mEq/L.
**What is the mechanistic explanation for this finding, and what does it suggest about future drug combinations in this unit?**

**Both the ACE inhibitor (by reducing aldosterone) and spironolactone (by directly blocking the aldosterone receptor) independently reduce potassium excretion — combined, and in the setting of CKD (which already impairs potassium excretion), the hyperkalemia risk compounds.**
**This is the same additive-risk logic that will reappear as the "triple whammy" in Session 2.** The ACEi/aldosterone-antagonist pair is one of three “whammies” formalized next session.

Recap: diuretic classes are organized by nephron site (Figure 2): loop diuretics (thick ascending limb) are most potent, followed by thiazides (distal tubule), then potassium-sparing and carbonic anhydrase inhibitors.
Recap: loop and thiazide diuretics have opposite effects on calcium excretion (Figure 3); potassium-sparing diuretics carry a hyperkalemia risk that compounds with ACE inhibitors or ARBs.

L10 · Renal Pharmacotherapeutics — Session 2 — study guide
**One pathway, four drug classes, and the preferred therapy for hypertension in CKD.** Today we follow the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, the pathway these drugs act on.

**Figure 8. Original illustrative diagram (not from Katzung): angiotensinogen is converted to angiotensin I by renin, then to angiotensin II by ACE; angiotensin II drives both vasoconstriction and aldosterone release.**
**Direct renin inhibitors, ACE inhibitors, ARBs, and aldosterone antagonists each block a different point in this cascade.**
This is the conceptual spine for the session: walk the cascade before naming drugs — angiotensinogen, renin, angiotensin I, ACE, angiotensin II, vasoconstriction and aldosterone.
ACE inhibitors: captopril, lisinopril, enalapril — "-pril" suffix across the class. ARBs: losartan, valsartan — "-sartan" suffix. Direct renin inhibitor: aliskiren.
g: L10 · Part 1 · Prototype + other drugs named

t: **Mechanism: block the conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II, reducing both vasoconstriction and aldosterone release (Figure 8).**

ACE also breaks down bradykinin: ACE inhibitor blocks ACE → less angiotensin II (less vasoconstriction and aldosterone) → less bradykinin breakdown, so bradykinin accumulates → cough or angioedema → switch to an ARB for cough.
ARBs block the AT1 receptor directly, rather than preventing angiotensin II formation. Aliskiren blocks the rate-limiting first step of the entire cascade.

Renoprotection: by reducing angiotensin II, these drugs preferentially dilate the efferent (outflow) arteriole of the glomerulus, lowering intraglomerular pressure and reducing proteinuria — a direct, structural renoprotective effect beyond systemic BP control.

Chain (Figure 10): angiotensin II normally constricts the efferent arteriole → ACE inhibitor or ARB removes that signal → efferent arteriole dilates; intraglomerular pressure falls → proteinuria falls; creatinine rises up to ~30%.
**ACE inhibitors and ARBs are first-line antihypertensive therapy in CKD, especially with proteinuria — not simply because they lower blood pressure.**
ARBs: no bradykinin-related cough — preferred alternative when ACE inhibitor cough is intolerable. ARBs do not raise bradykinin, so they are the usual switch.
Aliskiren: limited clinical use; useful mainly as a teaching example of where a drug could act upstream of ACE — included for conceptual completeness on Figure 8.
The drug class students might expect to avoid in kidney disease is actually the preferred therapy, precisely because of how it works at the glomerulus.
**Adverse effects: dry cough (bradykinin accumulation — the single most common reason for switching to an ARB), angioedema (rare but potentially life-threatening), and hyperkalemia.**

**Monitor potassium and renal function within 1–2 weeks of starting or up-titrating therapy, and periodically thereafter.**
**Hold or use with caution during acute illness causing volume depletion ("sick day rules") — combined with reduced renal perfusion, RAAS blockade can precipitate acute kidney injury.**

Sick-day rules: hold the ACE inhibitor or ARB during vomiting, diarrhea or dehydration. An early creatinine rise is expected and hemodynamic, not nephrotoxicity; a larger rise warrants checking for volume depletion or renal artery stenosis.

Case: a patient with hypertension and diabetic nephropathy is started on lisinopril; two weeks later serum creatinine has risen from 1.1 to 1.4 mg/dL. **Is this an indication to stop the ACE inhibitor?**
**A rise of roughly 27% is within the expected range for ACE inhibitor initiation, reflecting reduced intraglomerular pressure from efferent arteriolar dilation — not drug toxicity.**
**Therapy should generally continue with ongoing monitoring; a rise beyond approximately 30%, or a much sharper increase, should prompt evaluation for renal artery stenosis or volume depletion.**
A student who reflexively says "stop the drug" has missed that this creatinine rise is expected and even reflects the mechanism working as intended.

**RAAS blockers are first-line — but rarely the whole story.** Other major classes: CCBs, beta-blockers, diuretics, central agents and direct vasodilators.
This four-card slide is a brief classification recap — CCBs and beta-blockers get fuller treatment later this session (angina) and in cardiovascular coursework.

Calcium channel blockers: dihydropyridines (amlodipine) and non-dihydropyridines (diltiazem, verapamil). Beta-blockers: metoprolol, atenolol. Central α2 agonists: clonidine, methyldopa. Direct arteriolar vasodilator: hydralazine.

t: Dihydropyridines (amlodipine): arteriolar dilation. Non-dihydropyridines (diltiazem, verapamil): also ↓ HR/contractility.
Beta-blockers: ↓ heart rate, ↓ contractility, ↓ renin release.
Chain (Figure 11): dihydropyridine arteriolar dilation → afterload falls; blood pressure lowers. Non-DHP CCB or beta-blocker: heart rate and contractility fall → renin release falls.
Clonidine or methyldopa stimulates central α2 receptors → sympathetic outflow falls, so BP falls. Hydralazine dilates arterioles directly → reflex tachycardia and fluid retention.
Beta-blockers: not generally first-line for uncomplicated HTN, but compelling indications include concurrent CAD/heart failure/arrhythmia.

If all these classes lower blood pressure similarly, why are RAAS blockers preferred in CKD? Similar BP lowering; ACE inhibitors and ARBs add renoprotection — the renoprotective gap in Figure 12, not a difference in BP control.
Thiazide / loop diuretics (covered in depth in Session 1): thiazides first-line with preserved renal function; loops preferred as GFR falls.
Central agents (clonidine, methyldopa) and hydralazine: reserved for resistant hypertension or specific situations (e.g., methyldopa in pregnancy).
Diuretics enhance the efficacy of many agents, particularly ACE inhibitors; hydralazine and minoxidil need a diuretic because they cause salt and water retention.
Spironolactone may be the most effective single agent for drug-resistant hypertension.
Peripheral edema is a CCB class adverse effect.

**Resistant hypertension (BP above goal despite three or more antihypertensive classes, including a diuretic) is common in CKD, often driven by volume overload.**
First step: confirm diuretic therapy is adequate — a thiazide may simply no longer be effective at the patient’s current GFR (Session 1’s loop-vs-thiazide cutoff).
Switching from a thiazide to a loop diuretic, or increasing loop diuretic dosing, is often the most effective single change in advanced CKD.
**Aldosterone antagonists (spironolactone) can be added for resistant hypertension, but require close potassium and renal-function monitoring, especially on top of an ACE inhibitor or ARB.**

"Resistant hypertension in CKD" is often really a diuretic-selection problem, not a need for an entirely new drug class — check diuretic adequacy first; thiazide to loop switch; add spironolactone with close monitoring.

**Where cardiovascular and renal pharmacology converge — and where that convergence can go wrong.** This section covers vasodilators and angina, then the cardiorenal overlap.
**Figure 15. Original illustrative diagram (not from Katzung): angina results when myocardial oxygen demand exceeds supply; nitrates reduce preload, dihydropyridine CCBs reduce afterload,**
**non-dihydropyridine CCBs also reduce heart rate/contractility and increase coronary flow, and beta-blockers reduce heart rate and contractility.**
This figure organizes every antianginal drug class by exactly which side of the supply/demand equation it affects — sort nitrates, each CCB subtype, and beta-blockers onto it from memory.
Nitroglycerin (sublingual for acute angina; IV/patch for sustained use), isosorbide mononitrate/dinitrate (oral, longer-acting).

t: **Mechanism: release nitric oxide, activating guanylate cyclase and increasing cGMP, producing smooth muscle relaxation — predominantly venodilation at usual doses, reducing preload and myocardial oxygen demand.**
Chain (Figure 14): nitrate donates nitric oxide (NO) → NO activates guanylate cyclase, so cGMP rises → cGMP relaxes smooth muscle: venodilation → preload and oxygen demand fall.
**Dihydropyridines (amlodipine, nifedipine) — predominantly arteriolar dilation, reducing afterload; the same mechanism used for hypertension (Section 5).**

**Non-dihydropyridines (diltiazem, verapamil) — also reduce heart rate and contractility and increase coronary blood flow; avoid combining with beta-blockers due to additive bradycardia/AV block risk.**
CCBs are the clearest example in the unit of the same drug class, same mechanism, treating two different conditions (hypertension and angina).

This is the deliberate cardiovascular-renal "overlap" moment the lecture title promises — calcium channel blockers are not a separate topic from the antihypertensive content in Section 5; they are the same drugs doing double duty.
**Adverse effects: headache (vasodilation), reflex tachycardia, orthostatic hypotension.**

t: **Absolute contraindication: concurrent use with PDE5 inhibitors (sildenafil and similar) — the combination can cause life-threatening hypotension.**
PDE5 inhibitors such as sildenafil block cGMP breakdown, causing severe hypotension with nitrates.
The PDE5-inhibitor interaction is one of the highest-stakes medication-safety points in this whole unit — a real-world, repeatedly tested safety question worth a memorable callout.

**Figure 16. Original illustrative diagram (not from Katzung): an NSAID (afferent arteriolar constriction), an ACE inhibitor or ARB (efferent arteriolar dilation), and a diuretic (volume depletion) each independently reduce glomerular filtration pressure —**
**combined, the effect on kidney perfusion is additive to synergistic, substantially raising acute kidney injury risk.** An extremely common, often missed, entirely preventable cause of AKI.
Three hits (Figure 17): NSAID constricts the afferent arteriole → ACE inhibitor or ARB dilates the efferent arteriole → diuretic causes volume depletion → filtration pressure collapses: AKI.
NSAIDs blunt loop and thiazide action by reducing renal prostaglandins — significant in nephrotic syndrome or cirrhosis.
Tolerance develops with continuous exposure — a nitrate-free interval (typically overnight) is required to maintain efficacy with long-acting formulations.
Prevention: counsel patients about over-the-counter NSAIDs — ask which OTC NSAIDs they commonly take.
The triple whammy is the capstone cardiorenal interaction: Session 1’s diuretics + this session’s RAAS blockers + NSAIDs students will meet constantly in practice.
Hypertension → CKD: uncontrolled blood pressure causes glomerular capillary injury and nephrosclerosis over time — a leading cause of CKD progression, alongside diabetes.
CKD → hypertension: reduced renal function causes volume overload and RAAS activation, which worsens and complicates blood pressure control, often requiring multiple drug classes.

**Figure 18. Original illustrative diagram (not from Katzung): hypertension and chronic kidney disease drive one another in a self-reinforcing cycle — uncontrolled blood pressure causes glomerular injury and CKD progression,**
**while CKD causes volume overload and RAAS activation that worsens hypertension.**
Figure 18 is the conceptual closer for the whole unit — tie it back to Figure 8: RAAS blockade is effective precisely because it intervenes in both directions of this cycle at once.

Case: an older adult on lisinopril and hydrochlorothiazide starts a regular OTC NSAID for a knee injury; one week later, lethargy and an acute rise in creatinine. **What is the most likely explanation, and how could this have been prevented?**

**This is a classic "triple whammy" presentation (Figure 16) — the NSAID, ACE inhibitor, and diuretic each independently reduced glomerular filtration pressure, and together precipitated acute kidney injury.**
**Prevention requires counseling patients on RAAS blockers and diuretics to avoid regular NSAID use and to seek guidance before starting one, even an over-the-counter product.**
This case is the direct clinical application of Figure 16 and reinforces IO5.6 (patient counseling): the preventable element is entirely what the patient was or wasn’t told about OTC NSAID use.

Same patient, eGFR now 25: hydrochlorothiazide has likely lost much of its efficacy — switching to a loop diuretic (furosemide, torsemide) is more effective for blood pressure regardless of the NSAID issue.
Counsel the patient to avoid regular OTC NSAID use and to check with a prescriber or pharmacist before starting any new OTC product, given the RAAS blocker + diuretic combination already in place.

**Applying the whole Renal pharmacology toolkit.** Integration: put the drug classes together — for each patient, name a first-line approach AND the single biggest safety concern to check before prescribing or counseling.

**1.** Diuretic classes (Session 1) and RAAS-blocking antihypertensives both map onto specific, drug-targetable points in renal physiology — the nephron (Figure 1) and the RAAS cascade (Figure 8), respectively.
**2.** ACE inhibitors and ARBs are preferred first-line therapy for hypertension in CKD because of their renoprotective efferent-arteriolar mechanism, not just their blood-pressure-lowering effect.
**3.** Calcium channel blockers exemplify the cardiovascular-renal overlap directly — the same drug class, same mechanism, treats both hypertension and angina.
**4.** The "triple whammy" (NSAID + ACEi/ARB + diuretic) is a classic, common, and preventable cause of acute kidney injury that draws on content from both sessions at once.
**5.** Hypertension and chronic kidney disease exist in a bidirectional, self-reinforcing cycle (Figure 18) — which is exactly why managing one well so often means managing the other.
All three threads center on glomerular filtration pressure.

Connecting back to earlier units: drug-metabolism/dosing concepts (Unit 1) and the biologic-mechanism callbacks from Units 2–4 all reinforce that pharmacology is cumulative — the cardiorenal interface is where several organ-system units visibly intersect.
**Patient A — advancing CKD, hypertension no longer controlled on a thiazide:** switch to a loop diuretic; check potassium and volume status.
**Patient B — proteinuric CKD, needs first-line antihypertensive therapy:** ACE inhibitor or ARB; check potassium and creatinine in 1–2 weeks and pregnancy potential.
**Patient C — on an ACE inhibitor and a diuretic, about to start a daily OTC NSAID:** counsel against regular NSAID use — triple whammy AKI risk.

**Patient D — stable angina, already on a beta-blocker, needs additional symptom control:** add a dihydropyridine CCB or a long-acting nitrate; avoid diltiazem/verapamil (AV block) and PDE5 inhibitors with nitrates.
**A cumulative self-test spanning both sessions — use this to review before exams.** The recall quiz is a standalone resource, separate from in-lecture quick checks.

The **RAAS**: angiotensinogen → (renin) → angiotensin I → (ACE) → angiotensin II → vasoconstriction + aldosterone; aliskiren, ACE inhibitors, ARBs and aldosterone antagonists each block one step.

**ACE inhibitors/ARBs** are first-line in proteinuric CKD: efferent dilation lowers glomerular pressure; a creatinine rise **up to ~30%** is expected; check K⁺/creatinine in 1–2 weeks; **never in pregnancy**.

**The two core gonadal steroid classes, and how they are combined for contraception and hormone therapy.**

**Figure 2. Original illustrative diagram (not from Katzung): GnRH drives FSH/LH release, which drives gonadal sex-steroid production, which in turn negatively feeds back on the hypothalamus and pituitary —**

**with four distinct classes of drugs intervening at different points along this axis.** This is the organizing map for the session: GnRH agonists/antagonists, SERMs, aromatase inhibitors and antiandrogens each anchor to a point on it.
Estradiol and ethinyl estradiol (estrogens); norethindrone, medroxyprogesterone, levonorgestrel (progestins); combined oral contraceptives.
g: L11 · Part 1 · Prototype + other drugs named

t: **Mechanism: bind intracellular estrogen receptors (ER-alpha, ER-beta), regulating gene transcription in reproductive, bone, cardiovascular, and CNS tissue.**
Estrogen physiologic effects: endometrial proliferation, breast development, bone density maintenance, favorable lipid profile effects (↑ HDL, ↓ LDL).
**Mechanism: bind progesterone receptors, counteracting estrogen-driven endometrial proliferation and thickening cervical mucus.**

Unopposed estrogen chain (Figure 1): estrogen binds ER in the endometrium → proliferation and thickening of the lining → without progestin: hyperplasia and cancer risk → progestin binds PR: limits proliferation, matures the endometrium.
Unopposed estrogen drives unchecked endometrial proliferation; a progestin counteracts this proliferation.
Combined methods (oral pills, transdermal patch, vaginal ring) suppress ovulation via negative feedback on FSH/LH.
Estrogens raise hepatic clotting factors II, VII, IX and X and lower antithrombin III — the basis of the clotting risk; transdermal or vaginal routes avoid first-pass liver exposure.
Estrogen clinical uses: hormonal contraception (combined with a progestin), menopausal hormone therapy for vasomotor symptoms, and hypogonadism.
Progestins: a required component of combined hormonal contraception (protects the endometrium from unopposed estrogen), progestin-only contraception, and management of abnormal uterine bleeding.

Progestin-only methods — the "mini-pill," depot medroxyprogesterone acetate (DMPA) injection, the subdermal implant, and the levonorgestrel intrauterine system — avoid estrogen-related VTE risk entirely.
Combined methods are often chosen for added benefits: cycle regulation, acne/hirsutism improvement.
When estrogen is contraindicated, a progestin-only method is not a compromise — it is often the correct first choice (safe with VTE history, migraine with aura, or smokers over 35).
Postmenopausal hormonal therapy: vasomotor symptoms, genital atrophy and bone loss; after hysterectomy estrogen alone is fine because no progestin is needed.
An implantable progestin preparation (subdermal implant) provides long-acting progestin-only contraception.
Contraception with progestins alone suits patients with hepatic disease, hypertension, or prior thromboembolism.

**Adverse effects: venous thromboembolism (VTE) risk, increased risk with smoking and age over 35, nausea, breast tenderness, and a possible increase in certain hormone-sensitive cancer risks with long-term use.**

Contraindications & cautions: thrombophlebitis or past thromboembolism, cardiovascular or cerebrovascular disease, estrogen-dependent cancer, undiagnosed genital bleeding, liver disease.
Enzyme inducers (rifampin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, St. John’s wort) lower combined contraceptive efficacy.

The "unopposed estrogen" point is a classic exam item: any patient with a uterus receiving estrogen needs a progestin too, unless she has had a hysterectomy.
Beneficial effects of oral contraceptives: lower risk of endometrial and ovarian cancer, ovarian cysts and benign breast disease; lifetime breast cancer risk unchanged.
Mifepristone (RU-486) blocks progesterone and glucocorticoid receptors; 600 mg with misoprostol ends early pregnancy in over 95%.

**Tissue-selective and blocking strategies — how drugs can turn hormone signaling on in one tissue and off in another.**
A receptor-blocking strategy and a synthesis/activation-blocking strategy exist on both the estrogen and androgen sides.
Tamoxifen, raloxifene (SERMs); anastrozole, letrozole (aromatase inhibitors); testosterone; spironolactone, flutamide, bicalutamide (antiandrogens); finasteride, dutasteride (5-ARIs).

t: **Mechanism: bind the estrogen receptor, but act as an agonist in some tissues and an antagonist in others — the defining feature of this class.** Same receptor, different conformation and co-regulators in each tissue.
Tamoxifen: ER antagonist in breast tissue but an ER agonist in bone (preserves density) and, notably, in the endometrium. Tamoxifen antagonizes breast and agonizes bone and endometrium.

Raloxifene: ER antagonist in breast and ER agonist in bone, but — unlike tamoxifen — essentially neutral at the endometrium; tamoxifen is an ER agonist at the endometrium (raising endometrial cancer risk), both being ER antagonists in breast.

Aromatase chain (Figure 5): androgens (androstenedione, testosterone) → aromatase in fat tissue converts them to estrogens → estrogens drive ER-positive tumor growth → anastrozole and letrozole block aromatase.

**Figure 4. Original illustrative diagram (not from Katzung): SERMs block the estrogen receptor directly in breast tissue (while remaining agonists elsewhere), while aromatase inhibitors block the peripheral enzymatic conversion of androgens to estrogen —**
**two distinct strategies converging on the same clinical goal in hormone-sensitive breast cancer.** Receptor blockade versus synthesis blockade.
Androgen pathway (Figure 6): testosterone (circulating androgen) → 5-alpha-reductase converts it to DHT (more potent) → binds the androgen receptor → hair follicle and prostate effects.

Finasteride and dutasteride block 5-alpha-reductase, lowering DHT; spironolactone, flutamide and bicalutamide block the androgen receptor. Blocking the enzyme or the receptor both reduce androgen action — different mechanisms grouped under the same broad "antiandrogen" label.
Tamoxifen: ER-positive breast cancer treatment and prevention. Raloxifene: preferred option for osteoporosis prevention in postmenopausal women without a breast cancer indication.

Aromatase inhibitors block peripheral enzymatic conversion of androgens to estrogen rather than acting at the receptor — postmenopausal use only: before menopause the ovaries are the dominant estrogen source (often combined with ovarian suppression).
**●  Testosterone (androgen):** used for male hypogonadism.

**●  Spironolactone (antiandrogen):** blocks the androgen receptor (in addition to its aldosterone-antagonist diuretic effect from Unit 5) — used off-label for hirsutism and acne in women, especially in PCOS.
**●  Flutamide / bicalutamide (antiandrogens):** pure androgen receptor blockers used primarily in prostate cancer, often combined with a GnRH agonist (leuprolide).

**●  Finasteride / dutasteride (5-alpha-reductase inhibitors):** block conversion of testosterone to the more potent dihydrotestosterone (DHT); used for hirsutism and androgenetic alopecia here, and — in Session 2 — for benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH).
Estrogen-pathway drugs are used primarily in hormone-sensitive breast cancer; androgen-pathway drugs for hirsutism, prostate cancer, alopecia, and BPH.
Tamoxifen as adjuvant therapy cuts contralateral breast cancer by 35%; benefit does not grow beyond 5 years.
Clomiphene, a partial estrogen agonist, blocks hypothalamic feedback to trigger ovulation (mostly in PCOS); multiple pregnancy about 10%.
Other inhibitors: danazol suppresses the midcycle LH/FSH surge (endometriosis; hepatic caution); exemestane is an irreversible aromatase inhibitor.
**Tamoxifen’s endometrial agonist activity increases the risk of endometrial hyperplasia and endometrial cancer — patients require counseling on abnormal bleeding and routine gynecologic follow-up.**

Case: a 52-year-old postmenopausal woman with ER-positive breast cancer starts tamoxifen; six months later, new-onset irregular vaginal bleeding. **What is the most likely explanation, and what should happen next?**

**Tamoxifen acts as an estrogen receptor agonist in the endometrium even while acting as an antagonist in breast tissue — this tissue-selective agonism increases the risk of endometrial hyperplasia and endometrial cancer.**
**New abnormal bleeding on tamoxifen warrants prompt gynecologic evaluation, not reassurance.** A natural contrast with raloxifene’s neutral endometrial profile.

**Where Chapter 40 and Chapter 41 meet — insulin resistance as a driver of reproductive endocrine disease.**

**Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is defined by a combination of hyperandrogenism, ovulatory dysfunction, and polycystic ovarian morphology — but its pharmacologic management is fundamentally a metabolic problem as much as a reproductive one.**

**This is why PCOS management routinely pulls drugs from Chapter 41 (antidiabetic agents) as well as Chapter 40 (hormonal agents) — the two chapters converge on the same patient.** PCOS pharmacology is not purely "gynecologic."
Metformin; combined hormonal contraception; spironolactone; GLP-1 receptor agonists.

t: Insulin resistance and compensatory hyperinsulinemia are central to PCOS pathophysiology in most patients, independent of body weight.

Hyperinsulinemia stimulates ovarian theca-cell androgen production directly and lowers hepatic sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG) production, raising free (biologically active) testosterone — the mechanistic core of PCOS.

**Figure 7. Original illustrative diagram (not from Katzung): insulin resistance and hyperandrogenism reinforce one another in a self-sustaining cycle — hyperinsulinemia raises free testosterone, and hyperandrogenism worsens insulin resistance,**
**explaining why metabolic therapy improves reproductive symptoms and vice versa.** Walk both arrows of the cycle.

Metformin is not a direct hormonal agent — it improves hyperandrogenism indirectly, by reducing hyperinsulinemia’s stimulatory effect on ovarian androgen production (Figure 7) — by improving insulin sensitivity, not by acting on any hormone receptor.
Chain (Figure 8): insulin resistance → high insulin → ovarian androgens up; liver SHBG down → free testosterone up → metformin lowers insulin → androgens fall; cycles and ovulation can return.

Clinical features follow the mechanism: hirsutism, acne, and anovulation/irregular cycles from hyperandrogenism; an elevated long-term risk of type 2 diabetes and metabolic syndrome from insulin resistance.

**Metformin: first-line insulin-sensitizing agent in PCOS management; improves insulin sensitivity, can restore ovulatory cycles, and is commonly used alongside or instead of hormonal therapy depending on the patient's goals (cycle regulation vs. fertility).**
GLP-1 receptor agonists are increasingly used off-label in PCOS patients with obesity, given their weight-loss and insulin-sensitizing effects — an emerging extension of the same principle.

Combined hormonal contraception remains first-line specifically for cycle regulation and hirsutism/acne when pregnancy is not desired — metformin and hormonal therapy are frequently used together, not as alternatives.
Polycystic ovary syndrome affects about 7% of women of reproductive age.
**Adverse effects: GI upset (common, often transient), and rare but serious lactic acidosis risk in renal impairment — recall the renal dose-adjustment principles from Unit 5.**

Case: a 24-year-old with PCOS — irregular cycles, hirsutism, BMI 31 — not trying to conceive, no contraindications to estrogen. **What are the two major pharmacologic strategies available, and how do their goals differ?**

**Combined hormonal contraception directly regulates cycles and improves hirsutism/acne through its hormonal effects, while metformin addresses the underlying insulin resistance driving the condition metabolically.**
**The two are frequently combined rather than chosen as alternatives — contraception for immediate symptom control, metformin for the metabolic driver and long-term diabetes risk reduction.**

Drug names reveal the class: **Stem** · **Class** · **Examples** · **Memory aid** — estr-/-estradiol estrogen (estradiol, ethinyl estradiol); -gest-/-gestrel progestin (levonorgestrel, norethindrone, medroxyprogesterone: gest- = pregnancy hormone).

-ifene SERM (tamoxifen, raloxifene: modulates the estrogen receptor); -trozole aromatase inhibitor (anastrozole, letrozole: blocks aromatase); -steride 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor (finasteride, dutasteride: blocks steroid enzyme).

-lutamide antiandrogen (flutamide, bicalutamide: blocks the androgen receptor); -sterone androgen or antagonist (testosterone, spironolactone: steroid; drug sets the effect); -formin biguanide (metformin: lowers insulin).
Recap: **1.** Estrogens and progestins are always paired in a patient with a uterus — unopposed estrogen significantly raises endometrial cancer risk (Chapter 40).

**2.** SERMs and aromatase inhibitors are two distinct strategies for reducing estrogen signaling in hormone-sensitive breast cancer — tissue-selective receptor modulation (Figure 3) vs. blocking peripheral synthesis (Figure 5), compared in Figure 4.

**3.** Finasteride and dutasteride appear here for hirsutism and alopecia — the same drugs return in Session 2 for BPH. **4.** PCOS: insulin resistance and hyperandrogenism reinforce one another (Figure 7), so metformin and hormonal therapy are frequently combined.

**5.** Session 2 (Tuesday, December 1) shifts to autonomic pharmacology of the bladder and lower urinary tract — mechanistically different, but sharing cross-system drug-class connections with Units 5 and 6.

**Three nerve supplies, three receptor families — the physiologic foundation for every drug in this session.**
Parasympathetic M3 contracts the detrusor, sympathetic alpha-1 closes the bladder neck and beta-3 relaxes the reservoir, and somatic nicotinic control holds the external sphincter.

**Figure 9. Original illustrative diagram (not from Katzung): the parasympathetic, sympathetic, and somatic nervous systems each innervate a different structure of the lower urinary tract through a distinct receptor family —**
**the organizing map for every drug class covered this session.** Every class is anchored back to its receptor and anatomic location; Sections 5 and 6 "zoom in" on parts of this map.
Oxybutynin (blocks M3 on the detrusor), tamsulosin (blocks alpha1 at the bladder neck/prostate) and mirabegron (stimulates beta3 on the detrusor body) each target one receptor of this map.
g: L12 · Part 1 · Prototype + other drugs named

t: **The parasympathetic pelvic nerve releases acetylcholine, which acts on M3 muscarinic receptors on the detrusor muscle to produce contraction — the primary driver of bladder emptying (voiding).**
M3 is the dominant muscarinic subtype in the bladder, though M2 receptors are also present in high density (smaller functional contribution normally, may increase in disease).
Chain (Figure 10): pelvic nerve releases acetylcholine → ACh binds M3 on the detrusor → Gq activates phospholipase C; calcium rises → detrusor contracts and the bladder empties.
**M3 is the dominant bladder muscarinic subtype.** **M2 is more abundant but contributes less to contraction.** **Blocking M3 underlies antimuscarinic OAB treatment.**

**The sympathetic hypogastric nerve releases norepinephrine, which acts on two different adrenergic receptor subtypes in two different locations, producing two different (and complementary) effects.**
Chain (Figure 11): sympathetic hypogastric nerve releases norepinephrine → alpha-1: outlet closed; beta-3: reservoir relaxed → continence maintained during storage.
Alpha1 receptors at the bladder neck, trigone, and proximal urethra: norepinephrine causes contraction, helping maintain continence during storage.
Beta3 receptors on the detrusor body: norepinephrine causes relaxation, allowing the bladder to fill without a premature urge to void (low pressure).
**Because M3 blockade reduces detrusor contraction, antimuscarinic drugs (Section 5) are a logical treatment for conditions of bladder overactivity.**
**Both of these receptor subtypes become specific drug targets later in this session: alpha1 blockers for BPH (Section 6), and beta3 agonists for overactive bladder (Section 5).**

Net storage effect: sympathetic tone keeps the outlet closed (alpha1) while keeping the reservoir relaxed (beta3) — parasympathetic tone is low; both arms work together for continence. During voiding, this pattern reverses.
This is applied Chapter 6: the same muscarinic family that governs other smooth muscle and glands throughout the body — the bladder is simply one more target organ.
Know which receptor does what where (alpha1 at the outlet vs. beta3 on the detrusor body) before moving on — it makes the rest of the session’s pharmacology make sense.
Dominant tone · Storage phase: Sympathetic · Voiding phase: Parasympathetic

**Two mechanisms, one goal — calming an overactive detrusor to improve storage and reduce urgency.** Antimuscarinics block the detrusor’s muscarinic signal, while beta-3 agonists relax it.
**Figure 13. Original illustrative diagram (not from Katzung): antimuscarinics block the M3-mediated contraction signal, while beta3 agonists enhance the norepinephrine-mediated relaxation signal —**
**two distinct mechanisms converging on the same clinical goal of improved bladder storage.** Complementary, not competing — the basis for combination therapy.

t: **Mechanism: block M3 (and, to a lesser extent, M2) muscarinic receptors on the detrusor, reducing involuntary contractions and increasing functional bladder capacity.**
Antimuscarinic agents differ mainly in receptor selectivity and anticholinergic side-effect burden rather than core mechanism.

Chain (Figure 14): drug blocks M3 receptors on the detrusor → fewer involuntary contractions, larger capacity → same blockade in brain, salivary gland and bowel → bladder relaxes, but dry mouth, constipation and confusion follow.
Oxybutynin has the highest CNS anticholinergic burden; mirabegron, a beta-3 agonist, avoids this anticholinergic burden.

**Mechanism: stimulate beta3 adrenergic receptors on the detrusor, enhancing smooth muscle relaxation during the storage/filling phase.** Mirabegron is the primary beta3 agonist in clinical use for overactive bladder.
**Key advantage: lacks the systemic anticholinergic burden of antimuscarinics, making it a preferred option in older adults or patients already on multiple anticholinergic medications.**
Mirabegron can be used alone or combined with an antimuscarinic for refractory symptoms — complementary (not redundant) mechanisms.
**Adverse effects follow directly from systemic antimuscarinic blockade: dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision, and — importantly — cognitive impairment and confusion, especially in older adults.**

Case: a 78-year-old with mild cognitive impairment and urge incontinence starts oxybutynin; three weeks later, worsening confusion and new difficulty with daily tasks. **What is the most likely explanation, and what change in therapy would you consider?**
**Oxybutynin carries a relatively high CNS anticholinergic burden, and in an older adult — especially one with pre-existing cognitive impairment — this can precipitate or worsen confusion.**

**Switching to a beta3 agonist (mirabegron), which lacks anticholinergic activity, treats the same overactive bladder symptoms without this risk.** Review other anticholinergics too (medication reconciliation).
The anticholinergic-burden-in-older-adults point is the highest-yield safety point in this section; "no anticholinergic burden" is mirabegron’s single most important advantage.

**Where genitourinary pharmacology meets the cardiovascular system — alpha1 blockade, nitric oxide signaling, and a life-threatening drug interaction.** Alpha1 blockers relax the prostate; nitric oxide and cGMP drive erection.
Tamsulosin, silodosin, doxazosin, terazosin (alpha1 blockers); finasteride, dutasteride (5-ARIs); sildenafil, tadalafil, vardenafil (PDE5 inhibitors).
g: L12 · Part 3 · Prototype + other drugs named

t: **Mechanism: block alpha1 receptors at the bladder neck, prostatic smooth muscle, and proximal urethra, relaxing outflow resistance and improving urinary flow in benign prostatic hyperplasia.**

**Figure 14. Original illustrative diagram (not from Katzung): sympathetic norepinephrine normally contracts bladder neck and prostatic smooth muscle via alpha1 receptors, narrowing the outflow tract;**
**alpha1 blockers relax this same muscle to improve urinary flow — while the same receptor family elsewhere mediates vascular tone.**

**Mechanism: block 5-alpha-reductase, the enzyme that converts testosterone to the more potent dihydrotestosterone (DHT) — the same mechanism introduced in Session 1 for hirsutism and androgenetic alopecia.**
5-ARI chain (Figure 15): testosterone is converted by 5-alpha-reductase → the enzyme makes DHT → DHT drives prostate growth → enzyme blocked, DHT falls, prostate shrinks slowly.
**Figure 16. Original illustrative diagram (not from Katzung): non-adrenergic, noncholinergic (NANC) nerves release nitric oxide, raising cGMP and relaxing corpus cavernosum smooth muscle;**
**PDE5 normally terminates this signal by breaking down cGMP, and nitrates independently raise NO/cGMP systemically — the mechanistic basis for the absolute nitrate/PDE5-inhibitor contraindication.**

**Mechanism: block phosphodiesterase type 5 (PDE5), the enzyme that normally breaks down cGMP, prolonging smooth muscle relaxation in the corpus cavernosum and sustaining erectile function (Figure 16).**

Chain (Figure 17): sexual stimulation → NANC nerves release nitric oxide → guanylate cyclase makes cGMP → cGMP relaxes corpus cavernosum smooth muscle → erection. PDE5 breaks down cGMP and ends the signal.
Sildenafil, tadalafil and vardenafil block PDE5 and prolong the signal; an erection still needs sexual stimulation to start the pathway.
Tamsulosin, silodosin (more uroselective, less vascular effect) vs. doxazosin, terazosin (less selective, more likely to lower blood pressure systemically).
Finasteride, dutasteride: in BPH, reducing DHT shrinks prostatic tissue over time, improving urinary symptoms.

Onset: 5-ARI benefit typically takes 3–6 months, unlike the rapid onset of alpha1 blockers — the classes are frequently combined (alpha1 blocker for rapid relief, 5-ARI for long-term disease modification). Alpha1 blockers act in days; 5-ARIs take months.
PDE5 agents: sildenafil, tadalafil (longer half-life, allows more flexible dosing), vardenafil.
Finasteride is moderately effective in reducing prostate size in BPH; 1 mg/d is approved for early male pattern baldness.

**Adverse effects: orthostatic hypotension and a "first-dose effect" (pronounced hypotension with the first dose) — because alpha1 receptors also mediate vascular smooth muscle tone, not just bladder neck tone.**

t: **Absolute contraindication: concurrent use with any nitrate — both raise NO/cGMP signaling, and together they can cause profound, life-threatening hypotension.**

Why absolute rather than relative: nitrates and PDE5 inhibitors independently raise NO/cGMP signaling, and together can produce profound, life-threatening hypotension — pharmacodynamic and severe regardless of dose.
**This mirrors the identical nitrate/PDE5-inhibitor warning from Unit 5's angina content, now from the opposite side of the interaction.** Riociguat is also contraindicated with PDE5 inhibitors.
5-ARI pregnancy caution: finasteride/dutasteride can cause ambiguous genitalia in a male fetus; pregnant partners should avoid handling crushed or broken tablets.
Use caution with alpha1 blockers and PDE5 inhibitors together — additive hypotension, less severe than with nitrates, still warrants spacing doses or careful monitoring.

Nitrate + PDE5 inhibitor (Figure 18): nitrate raises NO and cGMP systemically → PDE5 inhibitor stops cGMP breakdown → together, vasodilation becomes profound → severe hypotension and syncope. Never combine.
Antihypertensives: additive hypotension with alpha-1 blockers. Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (ketoconazole, clarithromycin) raise PDE5 inhibitor levels.
Finasteride lowers DHT within 8 hours, lasting about 24 hours; dutasteride has a slow onset and a much longer half-life.
PSA falls about half on long-term 5-ARI therapy; read PSA accordingly.

**This is the exact same receptor family targeted by alpha1-blocking antihypertensives and central agents discussed in Unit 5 — the difference here is clinical intent (urinary flow vs. blood pressure), not a different drug class.**
Finasteride/dutasteride here are a deliberate callback to Session 1: same mechanism, same drugs, different clinical application.

Figure 16 applies the Chapter 6 non-adrenergic, noncholinergic neuron reading; the nitrate warning is the highest-stakes safety point in the unit — students saw it from the nitrate side in Unit 5, today from the PDE5 side.
Case: a 64-year-old with stable angina on isosorbide mononitrate asks for an ED prescription — a friend takes sildenafil "with no problems." Ask yourself: **What should the PA do, and why?**
**PDE5 inhibitors are absolutely contraindicated with any nitrate — both raise NO/cGMP signaling, and the combination can cause severe, life-threatening hypotension.**

**This prescription should not be written while the patient remains on a nitrate; the conversation should include alternative angina management or alternative ED options that do not involve this interaction, in consultation with his cardiologist.**
This case pulls a Unit 5 drug (isosorbide mononitrate) into a Unit 6 decision, making the shared NO-cGMP mechanism unmistakable.
