**Applying the whole genitourinary and reproductive pharmacology toolkit, across both sessions.**

**Figure 19. Original illustrative diagram (not from Katzung): the detrusor, bladder neck/prostate, and corpus cavernosum each rely on receptor families — muscarinic, adrenergic, and NO-cGMP signaling — that recur in the systemic vasculature,**
**explaining why so many genitourinary drug classes have direct cardiovascular counterparts or interactions.** Receptor families are shared with the vasculature — the unifying theme of the session.

Session 1’s gonadal hormone pharmacology (Ch. 40) and PCOS (Ch. 41 overlap) and Session 2’s autonomic bladder pharmacology (Ch. 6) are distinct but connect through shared classes — 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors appear in both sessions.
The lower urinary tract is governed by three nerve supplies and three receptor families (Figure 9): parasympathetic/M3, sympathetic/alpha1 and beta3, and somatic/nicotinic.

Antimuscarinics and beta3 agonists treat overactive bladder through complementary mechanisms — blocking contraction vs. enhancing relaxation — with anticholinergic burden the key safety differentiator in older adults.
Alpha1 blockers and 5-ARIs treat BPH through different timescales and mechanisms and are often combined; alpha1 blockade overlaps directly with Unit 5’s antihypertensive pharmacology.

The NO-cGMP pathway (Figure 16) underlies both erectile function and nitrate angina therapy (Unit 5) — therapeutic in one context, dangerous in combination in another: one of the highest-stakes safety points in the course.
Close by naming the cross-unit integration: genitourinary pharmacology shares receptor families and drug classes with cardiovascular pharmacology covered earlier in the course.
**Patient A — older adult with urge incontinence and mild cognitive impairment, needs therapy that avoids anticholinergic burden:** mirabegron (Section 5).
**Patient B — man with BPH, wants both rapid symptom relief and long-term disease modification:** combine an alpha1 blocker with a 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor (Section 6).
**Patient C — woman with PCOS, irregular cycles, and hirsutism, not currently trying to conceive:** combined hormonal contraception ± metformin (Session 1).

**Patient D — man with stable angina on a long-acting nitrate, requesting treatment for erectile dysfunction:** PDE5 inhibitors are contraindicated; this requires a cardiology-involved conversation about alternatives.
**A cumulative self-test spanning both sessions — use this to review before exams.**

Bladder map: **M3** contracts the detrusor (void); **alpha1** closes the neck and **beta3** relaxes the detrusor (store); somatic nicotinic holds the external sphincter.
**Antimuscarinics** block M3 — dry mouth, constipation, confusion; **oxybutynin** has the highest CNS burden → older adults get **mirabegron** (beta3; may raise BP).
**Alpha1 blockers** relax the outlet in days (orthostasis, first dose, floppy iris); tamsulosin/silodosin are uroselective.
**5-ARIs** shrink the prostate over 3–6 months and **halve PSA**; often combined with an alpha1 blocker.
**PDE5 inhibitors** keep cGMP high; **any nitrate = absolute contraindication** (and caution with alpha1 blockers).

t: Acetaminophen — Analgesic and antipyretic (not an NSAID)
Acetaminophen: Analgesia and antipyresis are mainly central (reduced CNS prostaglandin synthesis; hypothalamic temperature center); minimal peripheral anti-inflammatory action.
Acetaminophen: Textbook: a weak peripheral COX-1/COX-2 inhibitor; pain relief also involves opioid, cannabinoid, and serotonergic systems.
Acetaminophen: Mild-to-moderate pain and fever; reasonable first-line for mild osteoarthritis pain.
Acetaminophen: Preferred over aspirin in aspirin allergy, hemophilia, peptic ulcer history, or aspirin-induced bronchospasm; alone it is inadequate for RA.
Acetaminophen: Caution in liver disease, significant alcohol use, or malnutrition (prolonged fasting, anorexia).
Acetaminophen: Overdose: glutathione depleted → NAPQI accumulates → binds hepatocyte proteins → centrilobular liver necrosis.
Acetaminophen: Ingesting 15 g may be fatal; even 4 g/day is associated with liver function test abnormalities.
Acetaminophen: Combination cold, flu, and sleep products hide acetaminophen — unintentional double-dosing is a leading cause of liver injury. Ask about ALL sources.
Acetaminophen: Combined with an NSAID it improves pain control but can potentiate the NSAID’s GI toxicity.
Acetaminophen: Chronic alcohol use and fasting lower glutathione and induce CYP2E1 → higher toxicity risk.
Acetaminophen: Safer first-line than an NSAID when NSAID red flags (CKD, anticoagulant, older age) stack up.
Acetaminophen: Generic name — sold as Tylenol and many store brands; two brands can hide the same ingredient.
Acetaminophen: Metabolism: ~90% glucuronidation/sulfation (safe); ~5–10% CYP2E1 → NAPQI, neutralized by glutathione at therapeutic doses.

Acetaminophen: Acute single ingestion: plot a 4-hour-or-later level on the Rumack-Matthew nomogram — above the line, give N-acetylcysteine (early); check AST/ALT. Not used after 24 h or for chronic ingestion.
Acetaminophen: Normal Phase I metabolism makes the toxic metabolite NAPQI (Lecture 1’s example).
Acetaminophen: Adults generally no more than 4 g/day; half-life 2–3 h; N-acetylcysteine within 8–16 hours prevents fulminant hepatotoxicity.
Acetaminophen: Profile contraindications: Severe hepatic impairment; caution with chronic alcohol use
Acetaminophen: Toxicity/overdose: Hepatotoxicity from NAPQI after overdose; treat with N-acetylcysteine, ideally within 8 hours; use the Rumack-Matthew nomogram

Acetaminophen: Formulation: Tablets 325/500 mg; ER 650 mg; liquid; suppository; IV 1,000 mg. Adult dose: 650-1,000 mg PO every 6 hours (maximum 3-4 g/day; 2-3 g/day with chronic alcohol use or liver disease).
Albuterol — Selective β2-adrenergic receptor agonist
Albuterol: Binds and activates β2 → ↑ intracellular cAMP → bronchial smooth muscle relaxes → bronchodilation.
Albuterol: The lecture’s model for receptor-to-response logic you reuse for every agonist.
Warfarin — Anticoagulant
Warfarin: NSAIDs + anticoagulants → ↑ bleeding risk.
Warfarin: Inducers (barbiturates, St. John’s wort) lower its level; stopping the inducer raises it and can cause bleeding.
Warfarin: Celecoxib (CYP2C9 substrate) occasionally interacts; tocilizumab stimulates CYP450, so warfarin doses may need adjusting.
Warfarin: Dose requirements vary up to 20-fold; CYP2C9 and VKORC1 genotypes explain much of it.
Warfarin: Classic narrow-therapeutic-index drug — careful dosing and blood-level monitoring.
Warfarin: 99% protein-bound; half-life about 37 h.
Warfarin: Venous thromboembolism, atrial fibrillation, mechanical heart valves
Warfarin: Bleeding, bruising, hair loss, skin necrosis (rare)
Warfarin: Pregnancy (most cases), active bleeding, recent CNS surgery, uncontrolled hypertension
Warfarin: Toxicity/overdose: Hemorrhage; reversal with vitamin K and 4-factor PCC; many interactions (St. John's wort lowers INR)
Warfarin: Formulation: Tablet 1/2/2.5/3/4/5/6/7.5/10 mg. Adult dose: Start 2-5 mg PO daily, adjust to INR goal (usually 2-3).
Lithium
Lithium: Celecoxib raises lithium levels.
Lithium: Thiazides raise lithium levels — monitor.
Lithium: Renally cleared with a narrow TI — adjust dose or interval in renal impairment.
Lithium: Classic narrow-TI drug requiring blood-level monitoring.
Lithium: About 95% excreted unchanged in urine, 0% protein-bound; target ~0.7 mEq/L, toxic above 2 mEq/L; half-life ~22 h.
Digoxin
Digoxin: Inhibiting P-glycoprotein (MDR1) raises digoxin blood levels.
Digoxin: Hypokalemia from loop diuretics increases digoxin toxicity.
Digoxin: Renally cleared — adjust dose or interval in renal impairment.
Digoxin: Older adult with CrCl 22 mL/min: clearance falls to 3.7 L/h, so about 127 mcg/day (two 62.5-mcg tablets); draw levels at least 6 hours after a dose.
Digoxin: Classic narrow-TI drug requiring blood-level monitoring.
Digoxin: Very high Vd — mostly sequestered in tissue, not plasma.
Digoxin: Vd ~500 L, half-life ~39 h; target ~1 ng/mL, toxic above 2 ng/mL.
Phenytoin
Phenytoin: A CYP inducer — lowers levels of CYP substrates.
Phenytoin: Classic narrow-TI drug requiring blood-level monitoring.
Phenytoin: Capacity-limited (saturable) elimination — clearance falls as concentration rises.
Phenytoin: Target ~10 mg/L, toxic above 20 mg/L; 89% protein-bound.
Nitroglycerin — Organic nitrate
Nitroglycerin: Large first-pass effect — needs a higher oral dose or a non-oral route; sublingual dosing enters systemic veins directly, bypassing the liver.
Nitroglycerin: Releases nitric oxide → guanylate cyclase → ↑ cGMP → smooth-muscle relaxation, mainly venodilation → ↓ preload and O₂ demand.
Nitroglycerin: Acute angina, angina prophylaxis, acute heart failure, hypertensive emergency
Nitroglycerin: Headache, flushing, hypotension, reflex tachycardia, dizziness
Nitroglycerin: Concurrent PDE5 inhibitors (sildenafil, tadalafil) or riociguat, severe anemia, increased intracranial pressure, right ventricular infarction
Nitroglycerin: Toxicity/overdose: Severe hypotension and syncope, especially with PDE5 inhibitors; tolerance without a nitrate-free interval; methemoglobinemia at very high doses

Nitroglycerin: Formulation: Sublingual tablet 0.3/0.4/0.6 mg; spray 0.4 mg; patch 0.1-0.8 mg/h; IV infusion. Adult dose: Acute angina: 0.4 mg SL every 5 minutes up to 3 doses; patch 0.2-0.8 mg/h applied 12-14 hours per day; IV 5-10 mcg/min titrated.
Nitroglycerin: Acute angina: 0.4 mg SL every 5 minutes up to 3 doses.
Nitroglycerin: Absolute contraindication with PDE5 inhibitors (sildenafil) — life-threatening hypotension; nitrate-free interval prevents tolerance.
Nitroglycerin: PDE5 inhibitors or riociguat → severe hypotension.
Propranolol — Nonselective β-adrenoceptor antagonist (β blocker)
Propranolol: Competitive β antagonist: exercise or stress catecholamines can overcome a fixed dose.
Propranolol: Asthma: blocking β2 can cause bronchoconstriction — a β1-selective blocker is an alternative.

Dexamethasone: Insomnia, hyperglycemia, mood change, immune suppression
Dexamethasone: Systemic fungal infection, hypersensitivity
Dexamethasone: Toxicity/overdose: Potency about 25-30 times hydrocortisone with no mineralocorticoid effect; adrenal suppression, psychosis

Dexamethasone: Formulation: Tablet 0.5-6 mg; oral solution; IV 4/10 mg/mL. Adult dose: 0.5-9 mg PO or IV daily by indication; cerebral edema 10 mg IV load, then 4 mg every 6 hours; thyroid storm 2 mg IV every 6 hours.
Polyethylene glycol 3350 — Osmotic laxative
Polyethylene glycol 3350: Osmotic laxative: draws water into the lumen.
Polyethylene glycol 3350: Chronic and occasional constipation; bowel preparation (higher volumes)
Polyethylene glycol 3350: Bloating, nausea, gas, loose stools
Polyethylene glycol 3350: Bowel obstruction, perforation, ileus, toxic megacolon
Polyethylene glycol 3350: Toxicity/overdose: Dehydration and electrolyte loss with excess or bowel-prep volumes; rare allergic reactions
Polyethylene glycol 3350: Formulation: Powder for solution (17 g scoop); large-volume bowel-prep kits. Adult dose: 17 g in 4-8 oz fluid PO once daily; OTC use up to 7 days.
Polyethylene glycol 3350: First-line for chronic constipation; fast, reliable onset.
Psyllium — Bulk-forming laxative
Psyllium: Bulk-forming laxative: absorbs water, increases stool bulk and transit.
Psyllium: Constipation, IBS, mild cholesterol lowering
Psyllium: Bloating, gas, abdominal fullness
Psyllium: Bowel obstruction, fecal impaction, dysphagia
Psyllium: Toxicity/overdose: Esophageal or intestinal obstruction if taken with too little fluid; allergy; separate from other drugs by 2 hours
Psyllium: Formulation: Powder, capsules, wafers. Adult dose: About 3.4-6 g PO 1-3 times daily with at least 8 oz water.
Psyllium: Slowest onset, safest long term; needs adequate fluids; avoid in obstruction.
Methylcellulose — Bulk-forming laxative
Methylcellulose: Bulk-forming laxative: holds water and expands stool.
Methylcellulose: Constipation, stool bulking
Methylcellulose: Bloating, gas
Methylcellulose: Bowel obstruction, dysphagia
Methylcellulose: Toxicity/overdose: Obstruction if taken without adequate fluid; may slow absorption of other drugs
Methylcellulose: Formulation: Powder; caplets 500 mg. Adult dose: About 2 g PO in 8 oz water 1-3 times daily; onset 12-72 hours.
Lactulose — Osmotic laxative, ammonia-lowering agent
Lactulose: Osmotic laxative (nonabsorbable sugar): draws water into the lumen; also lowers ammonia.
Lactulose: Constipation, hepatic encephalopathy
Lactulose: Gas, bloating, cramps, diarrhea
Lactulose: Galactosemia, bowel obstruction
Lactulose: Toxicity/overdose: Dehydration and hypernatremia with over-use; worsens diabetes control slightly
Lactulose: Formulation: Oral solution 10 g/15 mL. Adult dose: Constipation: 15-30 mL PO daily; hepatic encephalopathy: 30-45 mL PO 3-4 times daily, titrated to 2-3 soft stools.
Senna — Stimulant laxative
Senna: Stimulant laxative: directly stimulates enteric nerves and motility.
Senna: Short-term constipation, opioid-induced constipation
Senna: Cramping, diarrhea, urine discoloration, melanosis coli
Senna: Bowel obstruction, appendicitis, undiagnosed abdominal pain
Senna: Toxicity/overdose: Hypokalemia and dehydration with chronic use; laxative dependence
Senna: Formulation: Tablet 8.6 mg sennosides; liquid. Adult dose: 8.6-17.2 mg PO at bedtime (max 34 mg/day); onset 6-12 hours.
Senna: Short-term or breakthrough use; cramping.
Bisacodyl — Stimulant laxative
Bisacodyl: Stimulant laxative: activates enteric nerves.
Bisacodyl: Constipation, bowel preparation
Bisacodyl: Cramping, nausea, rectal irritation
Bisacodyl: Bowel obstruction, appendicitis, acute abdomen
Bisacodyl: Toxicity/overdose: Do not crush; avoid with antacids or milk; excess causes diarrhea, hypokalemia
Bisacodyl: Formulation: DR tablet 5 mg; suppository 10 mg. Adult dose: 5-15 mg PO at bedtime; 10 mg PR once daily; PO onset 6-12 hours, PR 15-60 min.
Lubiprostone — Chloride channel (ClC-2) activator
Lubiprostone: Secretagogue: activates the ClC-2 chloride channel → more chloride and fluid secretion.
Lubiprostone: Chronic idiopathic constipation, IBS-C, opioid-induced constipation
Lubiprostone: Nausea, diarrhea, headache, abdominal pain
Lubiprostone: Mechanical GI obstruction
Lubiprostone: Toxicity/overdose: Dizziness, syncope or dyspnea (rare); overdose: nausea, diarrhea; avoid in pregnancy unless needed
Lubiprostone: Formulation: Capsule 8/24 mcg. Adult dose: Chronic constipation: 24 mcg PO BID with food; IBS-C (women): 8 mcg BID.
Lubiprostone: Nausea is the classic adverse effect.
Linaclotide — Guanylate cyclase-C agonist
Linaclotide: Secretagogue: guanylate cyclase-C agonist → more chloride and fluid secretion.
Linaclotide: Chronic idiopathic constipation, IBS-C
Linaclotide: Diarrhea, abdominal pain, gas, bloating
Linaclotide: Boxed: children under 2 years; mechanical GI obstruction
Linaclotide: Toxicity/overdose: Severe dehydration (deaths in young children); severe diarrhea; stop if severe or prolonged
Linaclotide: Formulation: Capsule 72/145/290 mcg. Adult dose: CIC: 72-145 mcg PO daily; IBS-C: 290 mcg daily; 30 minutes before the first meal.
Linaclotide: Diarrhea; contraindicated in mechanical obstruction and in children under 2.
Loperamide — Peripheral mu-opioid agonist
Loperamide: Peripheral mu-opioid agonist on enteric neurons → less acetylcholine → slower peristalsis, more water absorbed; enters the CNS poorly (P-gp efflux).
Loperamide: Acute and chronic diarrhea, traveler's diarrhea
Loperamide: Constipation, cramps, dizziness, nausea
Loperamide: Bloody stool or high fever, C. difficile, children under 2, ileus
Loperamide: Toxicity/overdose: High doses: QT prolongation, torsades, cardiac arrest; CNS depression in overdose (naloxone, repeated)
Loperamide: Formulation: Capsule 2 mg; tablet 2 mg; oral liquid. Adult dose: 4 mg PO first dose, then 2 mg after each loose stool; max 16 mg/day Rx, 8 mg/day OTC.
Loperamide: Avoid in suspected C. difficile and in bloody or febrile diarrhea; very high doses → QT prolongation.
Diphenoxylate/atropine — Opioid antidiarrheal (C-V) plus anticholinergic
Diphenoxylate/atropine: Opioid-receptor agonist slows motility; atropine at a subtherapeutic dose discourages misuse.
Diphenoxylate/atropine: Adjunct for diarrhea
Diphenoxylate/atropine: Drowsiness, dry mouth, tachycardia, urinary retention
Diphenoxylate/atropine: Children under 6 years, obstructive jaundice, C. difficile or infectious diarrhea
Diphenoxylate/atropine: Toxicity/overdose: Respiratory depression (especially children) and anticholinergic toxicity; naloxone, with monitoring for relapse
Diphenoxylate/atropine: Formulation: Tablet 2.5 mg/0.025 mg; oral liquid 2.5 mg/5 mL. Adult dose: 5 mg (2 tablets) PO QID initially; max 20 mg/day; reduce as controlled.
Diphenoxylate/atropine: Schedule V; avoid in young children and in infectious diarrhea.
Mesalamine — 5-ASA aminosalicylate
Mesalamine: 5-ASA: anti-inflammatory action local to the GI mucosa, reducing inflammatory mediators.
Mesalamine: Induction and maintenance in ulcerative colitis; mild Crohn disease (some forms)
Mesalamine: Headache, nausea, abdominal pain, flatulence
Mesalamine: Salicylate hypersensitivity
Mesalamine: Toxicity/overdose: Interstitial nephritis (monitor creatinine); acute intolerance syndrome (cramps, bloody diarrhea); hepatotoxicity rare

Mesalamine: Formulation: DR tablet 800 mg/1.2 g; capsule; suppository 1,000 mg; enema 4 g/60 mL. Adult dose: Mild-moderate UC: 2.4-4.8 g/day PO once daily or divided; 1,000 mg PR at bedtime for proctitis.
Mesalamine: First-line for mild-to-moderate UC; monitor renal function (interstitial nephritis); enemas/suppositories for distal disease.
Budesonide — Locally acting corticosteroid
Budesonide: Locally acting corticosteroid with high first-pass metabolism — less systemic exposure than prednisone.
Budesonide: Mild-moderate ileocecal Crohn disease, mild-moderate UC
Budesonide: Headache, nausea, acne, adrenal suppression with long courses
Budesonide: Hypersensitivity
Budesonide: Toxicity/overdose: Hypercortisolism with CYP3A4 inhibitors (ketoconazole, grapefruit juice); infection risk
Budesonide: Formulation: Capsule 3 mg; ER tablet 9 mg; foam. Adult dose: Crohn disease: 9 mg PO every morning for up to 8 weeks; UC: 9 mg ER tablet daily for 8 weeks.
Budesonide: Short-term induction of remission; not for maintenance.
Mercaptopurine — Purine antimetabolite
Mercaptopurine: Thiopurine: metabolized to thioguanine nucleotides that block purine synthesis in lymphocytes.
Mercaptopurine: Maintenance in Crohn disease and UC; acute lymphoblastic leukemia
Mercaptopurine: Nausea, leukopenia, hepatotoxicity, pancreatitis
Mercaptopurine: Hypersensitivity; use with febuxostat
Mercaptopurine: Toxicity/overdose: Myelosuppression, hepatotoxicity, lymphoma risk; reduce dose with allopurinol
Mercaptopurine: Formulation: Tablet 50 mg; oral suspension. Adult dose: IBD (off-label): 1-1.5 mg/kg PO daily after TPMT/NUDT15 testing.
Mercaptopurine: Test TPMT and NUDT15 first; allopurinol → cut dose by about two-thirds to three-quarters; monitor CBC and LFTs; onset weeks to months.
Vedolizumab — Humanized alpha4beta7 integrin antibody
Vedolizumab: Blocks α4β7 integrin-mediated leukocyte gut-homing — gut-selective, less systemic immunosuppression.
Vedolizumab: Moderate-severe ulcerative colitis and Crohn disease
Vedolizumab: Nasopharyngitis, headache, arthralgia, infusion reactions
Vedolizumab: Hypersensitivity
Vedolizumab: Toxicity/overdose: Infections and rare liver injury; PML not reported to date but vigilance advised; gut-selective with less systemic immunosuppression
Vedolizumab: Formulation: IV 300 mg vial; SC pen 108 mg. Adult dose: 300 mg IV at weeks 0, 2, 6, then every 8 weeks; SC 108 mg every 2 weeks after IV induction.
Vedolizumab: The IBD biologic that is most gut-selective.
Ustekinumab — Human anti-IL-12/23 antibody
Ustekinumab: Blocks interleukin-12 and -23 signaling.
Ustekinumab: Crohn disease, ulcerative colitis, psoriasis
Ustekinumab: Nasopharyngitis, injection-site reactions, headache, fatigue
Ustekinumab: Hypersensitivity
Ustekinumab: Toxicity/overdose: Serious infections, TB, reversible posterior leukoencephalopathy (rare), hypersensitivity
Ustekinumab: Formulation: IV 130 mg/26 mL vial; SC 45/90 mg. Adult dose: IV induction by weight (260 mg under 55 kg, 390 mg 55-85 kg, 520 mg over 85 kg), then 90 mg SC every 8 weeks.
Cyanocobalamin — Vitamin
Cyanocobalamin: Replaces vitamin B12 (absorption needs stomach acid to free it from food and intrinsic factor in the terminal ileum).
Cyanocobalamin: B12 deficiency, pernicious anemia, PPI or metformin-related deficiency
Cyanocobalamin: Injection-site pain, mild diarrhea, itching; early low potassium when treating severe anemia
Cyanocobalamin: Cobalt allergy, Leber hereditary optic neuropathy
Cyanocobalamin: Toxicity/overdose: Low toxicity; excess is excreted; folate alone can mask B12 anemia while neuropathy progresses
Cyanocobalamin: Formulation: Tablet 100-1,000 mcg; IM injection 1,000 mcg/mL; nasal gel. Adult dose: Deficiency: 1,000 mcg IM daily for 1 week, then weekly, then monthly; or 1,000-2,000 mcg PO daily.
Cyanocobalamin: Monitor B12 in long-term PPI or metformin users; treat with IM or high-dose oral B12.
Folic acid — Water-soluble vitamin
Folic acid: Replaces folate (water-soluble vitamin B9).
Folic acid: Megaloblastic anemia, pregnancy, sulfasalazine and methotrexate therapy
Folic acid: Nausea, bloating, rash (rare)
Folic acid: Untreated B12 deficiency (can mask anemia)
Folic acid: Toxicity/overdose: Low toxicity; high doses may mask B12 deficiency and worsen neurologic injury
Folic acid: Formulation: Tablet 0.4/0.8/1 mg; injection. Adult dose: Deficiency 1 mg PO daily; 0.4 mg daily for neural tube defect prevention (4 mg if prior NTD).
Folic acid: Critical in pregnancy to prevent neural tube defects.
Vitamin D — Fat-soluble vitamin
Vitamin D: Fat-soluble vitamin; deficiency impairs bone mineralization.
Vitamin D: Rickets, osteomalacia, osteoporosis support, deficiency
Vitamin D: Usually none; nausea and constipation with excess
Vitamin D: Hypercalcemia, hypervitaminosis D
Vitamin D: Toxicity/overdose: Toxicity: hypercalcemia, kidney stones, calcification; fat-soluble so accumulates
Vitamin D: Formulation: Capsule/tablet 400-5,000 IU; 50,000 IU capsule. Adult dose: Maintenance 600-800 IU PO daily; deficiency 50,000 IU weekly for about 8 weeks.
Phytonadione — Fat-soluble vitamin
Phytonadione: Vitamin K1: supports carboxylation of clotting factors II, VII, IX, X, opposing warfarin.
Phytonadione: Warfarin reversal, vitamin K deficiency bleeding, malabsorption
Phytonadione: Injection-site reactions; flushing
Phytonadione: Hypersensitivity
Phytonadione: Toxicity/overdose: IV: boxed warning for anaphylaxis (infuse slowly); overcorrection causes warfarin resistance
Phytonadione: Formulation: Tablet 5 mg; injection 10 mg/mL. Adult dose: Warfarin over-anticoagulation: 1-10 mg PO or slow IV by INR; newborn prophylaxis 0.5-1 mg IM.
Phytonadione: Warfarin patients: keep vitamin K intake consistent rather than avoiding it.
Ferrous sulfate — Iron supplement
Ferrous sulfate: Replaces iron; absorption enhanced by vitamin C, impaired by antacids and PPIs.
Ferrous sulfate: Iron-deficiency anemia
Ferrous sulfate: Constipation, nausea, dark stools, abdominal pain
Ferrous sulfate: Hemochromatosis, hemosiderosis, hemolytic anemia
Ferrous sulfate: Toxicity/overdose: Acute iron overdose is a pediatric emergency: GI bleeding, shock, liver failure; chelate with deferoxamine
Ferrous sulfate: Formulation: Tablet 325 mg (65 mg elemental); liquid. Adult dose: 325 mg PO once daily or every other day, ideally with vitamin C.
Ginkgo biloba — Herbal supplement
Ginkgo biloba: Herbal supplement that raises bleeding risk with anticoagulants/antiplatelets.
Ginkgo biloba: Self-treated memory complaints (limited evidence)
Ginkgo biloba: Headache, GI upset, dizziness
Ginkgo biloba: Bleeding disorders; stop before surgery
Ginkgo biloba: Toxicity/overdose: Increased bleeding with warfarin, antiplatelets, NSAIDs; seizures with seed ingestion
Ginkgo biloba: Formulation: Capsule/tablet 40-120 mg. Adult dose: 120-240 mg/day PO in divided doses; not FDA-approved for treatment.
Ginkgo biloba: Ask about supplements at every medication reconciliation.
Fish oil — Dietary supplement
Fish oil: Omega-3 fatty acids; raise bleeding risk at high doses with anticoagulants.
Fish oil: Hypertriglyceridemia, cardiovascular risk reduction (Rx)
Fish oil: Fishy aftertaste, belching, diarrhea
Fish oil: Hypersensitivity; fish or shellfish allergy (caution)
Fish oil: Toxicity/overdose: Bleeding risk at high doses with anticoagulants; atrial fibrillation at high doses
Fish oil: Formulation: Capsule 300-1,000 mg EPA/DHA; Rx icosapent ethyl 1 g. Adult dose: 1-4 g/day EPA plus DHA PO; Rx forms for hypertriglyceridemia.
Somatropin — Recombinant human growth hormone
Somatropin: Recombinant human growth hormone (replacement).
Somatropin: GH deficiency (children and adults), Turner syndrome, other growth disorders
Somatropin: Injection-site reaction, edema, joint pain, headache, hyperglycemia
Somatropin: Active malignancy, closed epiphyses (for growth promotion), acute critical illness
Somatropin: Toxicity/overdose: Fluid retention, glucose intolerance, intracranial hypertension, slipped capital femoral epiphysis; titrate by IGF-1
Somatropin: Formulation: SC injection pens and cartridges (several mg strengths). Adult dose: Adults: start about 0.2 mg SC daily and titrate by IGF-1; children: weight-based daily SC dosing.
Somatropin: Monitor growth velocity in children and IGF-1 in adults.
Octreotide — Somatostatin analog
Octreotide: Somatostatin analog: binds somatostatin receptors and lowers GH release (IGF-1 falls).
Octreotide: Acromegaly, carcinoid syndrome, VIPoma, esophageal variceal bleeding
Octreotide: GI upset, diarrhea, gallstones, bradycardia, glucose changes
Octreotide: Hypersensitivity
Octreotide: Toxicity/overdose: Gallstones, hypo- or hyperglycemia, bradycardia and conduction block; monitor IGF-1, glucose, gallbladder
Octreotide: Formulation: SC injection 50/100/500 mcg/mL; LAR depot IM 10/20/30 mg; oral capsule. Adult dose: Acromegaly: 50 mcg SC TID, titrate to 100-200 mcg TID; LAR 20 mg IM every 4 weeks.
Octreotide: Also variceal bleeding and carcinoid syndrome; GI upset, gallstones, bradycardia, glucose changes.
Lanreotide — Somatostatin analog
Lanreotide: Somatostatin analog: binds somatostatin receptors and lowers GH release (IGF-1 falls).
Lanreotide: Acromegaly, neuroendocrine tumors, carcinoid syndrome
Lanreotide: Diarrhea, abdominal pain, gallstones, injection-site reaction, bradycardia
Lanreotide: Hypersensitivity
Lanreotide: Toxicity/overdose: Gallstones, glucose dysregulation, bradycardia; monitor GH and IGF-1
Lanreotide: Formulation: Deep SC injection 60/90/120 mg prefilled syringe. Adult dose: 90 mg deep SC every 4 weeks for 3 months, then adjust between 60 and 120 mg.
Lanreotide: GI upset, gallstones, bradycardia; monitor IGF-1.
Pegvisomant — GH receptor antagonist
Pegvisomant: GH-receptor antagonist: blocks GH action so IGF-1 falls (GH itself rises).
Pegvisomant: Acromegaly not controlled by surgery or somatostatin analogs
Pegvisomant: Injection-site reaction, headache, raised liver enzymes, flu-like symptoms
Pegvisomant: Hypersensitivity
Pegvisomant: Toxicity/overdose: Liver injury; monitor tumor size by MRI; GH levels rise and are not used for monitoring
Pegvisomant: Formulation: SC injection vials 10/15/20/25/30 mg. Adult dose: Load 40 mg SC, then 10 mg SC daily, titrate by IGF-1 (max 30 mg/day).
Pegvisomant: Does not shrink the tumor; monitor IGF-1 (not GH) and liver tests.
Cabergoline — Dopamine D2 agonist (ergot-derived)
Cabergoline: Dopamine D2 agonist (ergot-derived): restores dopamine’s brake on prolactin; tumor often shrinks.
Cabergoline: Hyperprolactinemia, prolactinoma
Cabergoline: Nausea, dizziness, headache, orthostatic hypotension
Cabergoline: Uncontrolled hypertension, cardiac valvulopathy, ergot hypersensitivity
Cabergoline: Toxicity/overdose: Cardiac valve fibrosis at high doses; impulse-control and psychiatric effects; overdose causes hypotension and nausea
Cabergoline: Formulation: Tablet 0.5 mg. Adult dose: 0.25 mg PO twice weekly, increase by 0.25 mg every 4 weeks to usual max 1 mg twice weekly.
Cabergoline: Twice weekly, better tolerated; high doses (Parkinson) linked to valve fibrosis; nausea, orthostasis.
Cabergoline: Antipsychotics and metoclopramide raise prolactin.
Bromocriptine — Dopamine D2 agonist (ergot-derived)
Bromocriptine: Dopamine D2 agonist (ergot-derived): restores dopamine’s brake on prolactin; tumor often shrinks.
Bromocriptine: Hyperprolactinemia, acromegaly (adjunct), Parkinson disease, type 2 diabetes (Cycloset)
Bromocriptine: Nausea, orthostatic hypotension, dizziness, headache, nasal congestion
Bromocriptine: Uncontrolled hypertension, pregnancy-related hypertension, ergot hypersensitivity
Bromocriptine: Toxicity/overdose: Hypotension and syncope, psychosis, fibrosis with long-term high doses; take with food
Bromocriptine: Formulation: Tablet 2.5 mg; capsule 5 mg; Cycloset 0.8 mg tablet. Adult dose: 1.25-2.5 mg PO at bedtime, titrate to 2.5 mg BID-TID for prolactinoma (max 15 mg/day).
Bromocriptine: Daily dosing; nausea, orthostatic hypotension, dizziness.
Bromocriptine: Antipsychotics and metoclopramide raise prolactin.
Desmopressin — Synthetic vasopressin V2 agonist
Desmopressin: Synthetic vasopressin V2 agonist: aquaporin-2 insertion → free water retained.
Desmopressin: Central diabetes insipidus, nocturnal enuresis, hemophilia A and von Willebrand disease (IV)
Desmopressin: Headache, nausea, flushing, hyponatremia
Desmopressin: Hyponatremia history, polydipsia, eGFR below 50, heart failure
Desmopressin: Toxicity/overdose: Water intoxication with severe hyponatremia and seizures; limit fluids and monitor sodium

Desmopressin: Formulation: Tablet 0.1/0.2 mg; nasal spray; SC/IV 4 mcg/mL; ODT 60 mcg. Adult dose: Central DI: 0.05-0.2 mg PO BID, or 10-40 mcg intranasal daily in divided doses; titrate to urine output.
Desmopressin: Central DI; risk is hyponatremia — monitor sodium and limit fluids.
Tolvaptan — Vasopressin V2 receptor antagonist
Tolvaptan: Vasopressin V2 receptor antagonist: free water excreted (aquaresis).
Tolvaptan: Hyponatremia from SIADH or heart failure
Tolvaptan: Thirst, dry mouth, polyuria, hypernatremia, liver injury
Tolvaptan: Urgent need to raise sodium, hypovolemia, anuria, strong CYP3A4 inhibitors
Tolvaptan: Toxicity/overdose: Overly rapid sodium correction (osmotic demyelination); liver injury; limit therapy to 30 days
Tolvaptan: Formulation: Tablet 15/30 mg. Adult dose: 15 mg PO once daily, titrate to 30-60 mg; start in hospital.
Tolvaptan: SIADH refractory to fluid restriction; overcorrection (osmotic demyelination) and liver injury — start in hospital.
Demeclocycline — Tetracycline with ADH-antagonist effect
Demeclocycline: Tetracycline that blunts ADH action in the collecting duct.
Demeclocycline: Refractory SIADH (off-label), bacterial infections
Demeclocycline: Photosensitivity, nausea, nephrogenic diabetes insipidus
Demeclocycline: Pregnancy, children under 8 years, hypersensitivity, severe renal impairment
Demeclocycline: Toxicity/overdose: Nephrotoxicity, photosensitivity, tooth discoloration; separate from calcium and antacids
Demeclocycline: Formulation: Tablet 150/300 mg. Adult dose: 150-300 mg PO 3-4 times daily for SIADH (off-label).
Demeclocycline: Refractory SIADH; photosensitivity and nephrotoxicity.
Levothyroxine — Synthetic thyroid hormone (T4)
Levothyroxine: Synthetic T4, converted peripherally to active T3, which binds nuclear receptors.
Levothyroxine: Hypothyroidism, myxedema coma (IV), TSH suppression in thyroid cancer
Levothyroxine: Usually none at the right dose; over-replacement causes tachycardia, tremor, insomnia, bone loss
Levothyroxine: Uncorrected adrenal insufficiency, acute MI, hypersensitivity
Levothyroxine: Toxicity/overdose: Over-replacement: atrial fibrillation, angina, osteoporosis; separate from calcium, iron and antacids by 4 hours

Levothyroxine: Formulation: Tablet 25-300 mcg (12 strengths); IV 100-500 mcg vial; liquid and capsule. Adult dose: Full replacement about 1.6 mcg/kg/day PO; start 12.5-50 mcg in older adults or heart disease; recheck TSH in 6-8 weeks.
Levothyroxine: Empty stomach 30–60 min before breakfast; separate calcium, iron, antacids, PPIs, binders by 4 h; TSH at 6–8 weeks.
Levothyroxine: Start low in older adults and cardiac disease; over-replacement → AF, bone loss; pregnancy raises needs.
Levothyroxine: Calcium, iron, antacids block absorption; estrogens raise needs; rifampin, phenytoin, carbamazepine speed clearance.
Methimazole — Thionamide antithyroid drug
Methimazole: Thionamide: blocks thyroid hormone organification and coupling.
Methimazole: Graves disease, toxic nodular goiter, pre-operative control
Methimazole: Rash, itching, joint pain, taste change; agranulocytosis (rare)
Methimazole: First trimester of pregnancy; prior methimazole agranulocytosis
Methimazole: Toxicity/overdose: Agranulocytosis (fever or sore throat: stop and check CBC), hepatotoxicity, teratogenicity
Methimazole: Formulation: Tablet 5/10 mg. Adult dose: Graves disease: start 10-30 mg PO once daily; adjust to free T4 every 4-6 weeks.
Methimazole: First line for most non-pregnant patients (once daily); avoid in first trimester; agranulocytosis and liver boxed warning — fever or sore throat → CBC.
Propylthiouracil — Thionamide antithyroid drug (also blocks T4 to T3)
Propylthiouracil: Thionamide: blocks organification and coupling and also peripheral T4 → T3 conversion.
Propylthiouracil: First-trimester Graves disease, thyroid storm, methimazole intolerance
Propylthiouracil: Rash, nausea, taste change, joint pain
Propylthiouracil: Prior PTU liver injury; avoid in children
Propylthiouracil: Toxicity/overdose: Boxed warning: severe liver failure; agranulocytosis; ANCA-positive vasculitis
Propylthiouracil: Formulation: Tablet 50 mg. Adult dose: Start 100 mg PO TID (up to 300-400 mg/day); thyroid storm: 500-1,000 mg load, then 250 mg every 4 hours.
Propylthiouracil: First trimester and thyroid storm only — severe hepatotoxicity boxed warning.
Potassium iodide — Iodine (blocks hormone release)
Potassium iodide: Iodine: acutely blocks thyroid hormone release (Wolff-Chaikoff).
Potassium iodide: Thyroid storm, pre-thyroidectomy preparation, radiation protection
Potassium iodide: Metallic taste, GI upset, salivary gland swelling, rash
Potassium iodide: Giving before a thionamide; iodine allergy
Potassium iodide: Toxicity/overdose: Iodism (rash, swelling, fever); thyroid escape after about 10 days; hypo- or hyperthyroidism
Potassium iodide: Formulation: SSKI 1 g/mL solution; Lugol 5% solution; tablets 65/130 mg. Adult dose: Thyroid storm: 5 drops (about 250 mg) SSKI PO every 6 hours, at least 1 hour after a thionamide.
Potassium iodide: Thyroid storm: give at least 1 hour after a thionamide — never first (supplies substrate).
Hydrocortisone — Glucocorticoid with mineralocorticoid activity
Hydrocortisone: Cortisol: glucocorticoid with mineralocorticoid activity.
Hydrocortisone: Adrenal insufficiency, adrenal crisis, inflammatory conditions
Hydrocortisone: Hyperglycemia, fluid retention, mood change, infection risk
Hydrocortisone: Systemic fungal infection
Hydrocortisone: Toxicity/overdose: Excess causes Cushingoid features, hypertension, hypokalemia; stress-dose during illness and surgery
Hydrocortisone: Formulation: Tablet 5/10/20 mg; IV 100 mg vial. Adult dose: Replacement 15-25 mg/day PO in 2-3 divided doses; adrenal crisis 100 mg IV, then 200 mg over 24 hours.
Hydrocortisone: Adrenal crisis: immediate IV hydrocortisone plus IV fluids.
Hydrocortisone: Chronic use suppresses CRH/ACTH — taper, never stop abruptly; hyperglycemia, osteoporosis, infection, mood change, cataracts.
Hydrocortisone: Azole antifungals raise exposure (CYP3A4); insulin and oral agents need adjusting.
Fludrocortisone — Mineralocorticoid
Fludrocortisone: Mineralocorticoid: renal sodium retention and potassium excretion.
Fludrocortisone: Primary adrenal insufficiency (with a glucocorticoid), orthostatic hypotension
Fludrocortisone: Hypertension, edema, hypokalemia, headache
Fludrocortisone: Systemic fungal infection; caution in heart failure
Fludrocortisone: Toxicity/overdose: Hypokalemia, fluid overload, supine hypertension; monitor blood pressure and potassium
Fludrocortisone: Formulation: Tablet 0.1 mg. Adult dose: 0.05-0.2 mg PO once daily.
Fludrocortisone: Addison disease with a glucocorticoid; monitor blood pressure and potassium.
Metyrapone — 11-beta-hydroxylase inhibitor
Metyrapone: Blocks 11-β-hydroxylase, the final step of cortisol synthesis.
Metyrapone: Cushing syndrome, diagnostic test of the HPA axis
Metyrapone: Nausea, dizziness, hypertension, edema, hirsutism
Metyrapone: Adrenal insufficiency, hypersensitivity
Metyrapone: Toxicity/overdose: Adrenal insufficiency, hypokalemia, hypertension from deoxycorticosterone, androgen excess
Metyrapone: Formulation: Capsule 250 mg. Adult dose: Cushing syndrome: start 250 mg PO TID-QID, titrate to cortisol (up to 6 g/day); diagnostic test: 30 mg/kg once at midnight.
Metyrapone: Cushing syndrome and diagnostic testing; raises androgens and deoxycorticosterone.
Mifepristone — Glucocorticoid-receptor antagonist

Hydralazine: Direct arteriolar vasodilator → reflex tachycardia and fluid retention.
Hydralazine: Resistant hypertension, hypertensive emergency in pregnancy, heart failure (with nitrate)
Hydralazine: Headache, reflex tachycardia, fluid retention, flushing, drug-induced lupus
Hydralazine: Coronary artery disease without beta-blocker, mitral valve rheumatic disease, hypersensitivity
Hydralazine: Toxicity/overdose: Reflex tachycardia, angina, lupus-like syndrome with high dose or slow acetylators; pair with beta-blocker and diuretic

Hydralazine: Formulation: Tablets 10/25/50/100 mg; IV injection. Adult dose: Hypertension: 10 mg PO QID, titrate to 25-50 mg QID (maximum 300 mg/day); heart failure with isosorbide dinitrate: 25-75 mg TID.
Hydralazine: Must be paired with a beta-blocker and a diuretic; drug-induced lupus.
Isosorbide mononitrate — Organic nitrate (long-acting)
Isosorbide mononitrate: Releases nitric oxide → guanylate cyclase → ↑ cGMP → smooth-muscle relaxation, mainly venodilation → ↓ preload and O₂ demand.
Isosorbide mononitrate: Angina prophylaxis
Isosorbide mononitrate: Headache, dizziness, hypotension, flushing
Isosorbide mononitrate: Concurrent PDE5 inhibitors or riociguat, severe anemia, increased intracranial pressure
Isosorbide mononitrate: Toxicity/overdose: Hypotension, headache; tolerance requires nitrate-free interval

Isosorbide mononitrate: Formulation: ER tablets 30/60/120 mg; immediate-release tablets 10/20 mg. Adult dose: ER: 30-60 mg PO every morning, up to 240 mg/day; immediate-release: 20 mg BID given 7 hours apart.
Isosorbide mononitrate: Absolute contraindication with PDE5 inhibitors (sildenafil) — life-threatening hypotension; nitrate-free interval prevents tolerance.
Isosorbide mononitrate: PDE5 inhibitors or riociguat → severe hypotension.
Isosorbide dinitrate — Organic nitrate
Isosorbide dinitrate: Releases nitric oxide → guanylate cyclase → ↑ cGMP → smooth-muscle relaxation, mainly venodilation → ↓ preload and O₂ demand.
Isosorbide dinitrate: Angina prophylaxis, heart failure in Black patients (with hydralazine)
Isosorbide dinitrate: Headache, flushing, hypotension, reflex tachycardia
Isosorbide dinitrate: Concurrent PDE5 inhibitors or riociguat, severe anemia, increased intracranial pressure
Isosorbide dinitrate: Toxicity/overdose: Hypotension, syncope, headache; tolerance without a nitrate-free interval

Isosorbide dinitrate: Formulation: Tablets 5/10/20/30/40 mg; ER capsules 40 mg; combination with hydralazine (BiDil). Adult dose: Angina: 10-40 mg PO TID with a 14-hour nitrate-free interval; heart failure: 20-40 mg TID with hydralazine.
Isosorbide dinitrate: Absolute contraindication with PDE5 inhibitors (sildenafil) — life-threatening hypotension; nitrate-free interval prevents tolerance.
Isosorbide dinitrate: With hydralazine for heart failure in Black patients.
Isosorbide dinitrate: PDE5 inhibitors or riociguat → severe hypotension.
Estradiol — Estrogen
Estradiol: Binds intracellular estrogen receptors (ER-α, ER-β) → gene transcription in reproductive, bone, cardiovascular and CNS tissue.
Estradiol: Menopausal vasomotor symptoms, genitourinary syndrome of menopause, hypoestrogenism, prevention of osteoporosis (when other agents unsuitable)
Estradiol: Breast tenderness, nausea, headache, VTE, stroke, endometrial hyperplasia (unopposed), gallbladder disease
Estradiol: History of VTE or stroke, estrogen-sensitive cancer, undiagnosed vaginal bleeding, active liver disease, pregnancy

Anastrozole: Aromatase inhibitor: blocks peripheral (fat) conversion of androgens to estrogens.
Anastrozole: Adjuvant and metastatic hormone receptor-positive breast cancer in postmenopausal women
Anastrozole: Hot flashes, joint pain, bone loss, osteoporosis, mood changes, hypercholesterolemia

Anastrozole: Toxicity/overdose: Bone loss and fractures; monitor bone density and lipids; overdose causes mainly GI upset
Anastrozole: Formulation: Tablets 1 mg. Adult dose: 1 mg PO once daily, usually for 5 years or more.
Anastrozole: Postmenopausal only (ovaries still make estrogen before menopause); bone loss and joint pain — protect bone.
Anastrozole: Bisphosphonates and calcium with vitamin D protect bone.
Letrozole — Aromatase inhibitor
Letrozole: Aromatase inhibitor: blocks peripheral conversion of androgens to estrogens.
Letrozole: Hormone receptor-positive breast cancer in postmenopausal women; off-label ovulation induction
Letrozole: Hot flashes, arthralgia, osteoporosis, fatigue, hypercholesterolemia
Letrozole: Pregnancy; premenopausal status without ovarian suppression
Letrozole: Toxicity/overdose: Bone loss and fractures; monitor bone density; nonspecific toxicity in overdose
Letrozole: Formulation: Tablets 2.5 mg. Adult dose: 2.5 mg PO once daily, up to 5 years or extended therapy.
Letrozole: Postmenopausal only; bone loss and joint pain; off-label ovulation induction.
Letrozole: Bisphosphonates and calcium with vitamin D protect bone.
Flutamide — Nonsteroidal antiandrogen
Flutamide: Pure androgen-receptor blocker.
Flutamide: Metastatic prostate cancer in combination with a GnRH agonist
Flutamide: Hot flashes, gynecomastia, diarrhea, hepatotoxicity, methemoglobinemia
Flutamide: Severe hepatic impairment, pregnancy
Flutamide: Toxicity/overdose: Boxed warning for severe hepatotoxicity; monitor liver tests regularly
Flutamide: Formulation: Capsules 125 mg. Adult dose: 250 mg PO three times daily, given with a GnRH agonist in prostate cancer.
Flutamide: Prostate cancer, often with a GnRH agonist; gynecomastia and reversible hepatotoxicity.
Flutamide: Combined with a GnRH agonist in prostate cancer.
Bicalutamide — Nonsteroidal antiandrogen
Bicalutamide: Pure androgen-receptor blocker (once daily).
Bicalutamide: Metastatic prostate cancer in combination with a GnRH agonist
Bicalutamide: Hot flashes, gynecomastia, breast tenderness, fatigue, liver enzyme elevation
Bicalutamide: Pregnancy (not indicated in women), severe hepatic impairment
Bicalutamide: Toxicity/overdose: Hepatotoxicity (rare); monitor liver tests; potentiates warfarin
Bicalutamide: Formulation: Tablets 50 mg (150 mg in some regions). Adult dose: 50 mg PO once daily with a GnRH agonist in prostate cancer.
Bicalutamide: Prostate cancer with a GnRH analog (leuprolide) to prevent tumor flare.
Bicalutamide: Combined with leuprolide (GnRH agonist) in prostate cancer.

Dutasteride: 5-alpha-reductase (types 1 and 2) inhibitor: blocks testosterone → DHT.

Oxybutynin — Antimuscarinic (overactive bladder)
Oxybutynin: Antimuscarinic: blocks M3 (and M2) receptors on the detrusor → fewer involuntary contractions, larger functional capacity.
Oxybutynin: Overactive bladder, urge incontinence, neurogenic bladder
Oxybutynin: Dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision, drowsiness, confusion, urinary retention
Oxybutynin: Narrow-angle glaucoma, urinary retention, gastric retention, severe ulcerative colitis; avoid in older adults with dementia
Oxybutynin: Toxicity/overdose: Anticholinergic toxicity: confusion, hallucinations, tachycardia, hyperthermia, urinary retention; highest CNS burden in the class

Oxybutynin: Highest CNS anticholinergic burden of the class — avoid in older adults or dementia risk; switch to mirabegron if confused.
Oxybutynin: Dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision, confusion (older adults); anticholinergic burden is cumulative; avoid in narrow-angle glaucoma and urinary retention.
Oxybutynin: Other anticholinergics add burden; cholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil) oppose the effect.
Tolterodine — Antimuscarinic
Tolterodine: Antimuscarinic: blocks M3 (and M2) receptors on the detrusor → fewer involuntary contractions, larger functional capacity.
Tolterodine: Overactive bladder with urgency, frequency, and urge incontinence
Tolterodine: Dry mouth, constipation, headache, dizziness, dry eyes, QT prolongation (rare)
Tolterodine: Urinary retention, gastric retention, uncontrolled narrow-angle glaucoma
Tolterodine: Toxicity/overdose: Anticholinergic toxicity; reduce dose with CYP3A4 inhibitors or hepatic impairment
Tolterodine: Formulation: Tablets 1/2 mg; ER capsules 2/4 mg. Adult dose: IR: 2 mg PO twice daily (1 mg if hepatic impairment or strong CYP3A4 inhibitors); ER: 4 mg daily.
Tolterodine: Dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision, confusion (older adults); anticholinergic burden is cumulative; avoid in narrow-angle glaucoma and urinary retention.
Tolterodine: Other anticholinergics add burden; cholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil) oppose the effect.
Solifenacin — Antimuscarinic (M3-selective)
Solifenacin: Antimuscarinic: blocks M3 (and M2) receptors on the detrusor → fewer involuntary contractions, larger functional capacity.
Solifenacin: Overactive bladder
Solifenacin: Dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision, QT prolongation, urinary retention
Solifenacin: Urinary retention, gastric retention, uncontrolled narrow-angle glaucoma
Solifenacin: Toxicity/overdose: Anticholinergic toxicity and QT prolongation in overdose; adjust dose with kidney, liver, and CYP3A4 interactions
Solifenacin: Formulation: Tablets 5/10 mg. Adult dose: 5 mg PO once daily, may increase to 10 mg (maximum 5 mg with severe renal impairment or strong CYP3A4 inhibitors).
Solifenacin: Dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision, confusion (older adults); anticholinergic burden is cumulative; avoid in narrow-angle glaucoma and urinary retention.
Solifenacin: Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors raise levels.
Solifenacin: Other anticholinergics add burden; cholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil) oppose the effect.
Darifenacin — Antimuscarinic (M3-selective)
Darifenacin: Antimuscarinic: blocks M3 (and M2) receptors on the detrusor → fewer involuntary contractions, larger functional capacity.
Darifenacin: Overactive bladder
Darifenacin: Constipation (prominent), dry mouth, dyspepsia, headache
Darifenacin: Urinary or gastric retention, uncontrolled narrow-angle glaucoma
Darifenacin: Toxicity/overdose: Anticholinergic toxicity; CYP2D6 and CYP3A4 interactions; limit dose with moderate CYP3A4 inhibitors
Darifenacin: Formulation: ER tablets 7.5/15 mg. Adult dose: 7.5 mg PO once daily, may increase to 15 mg after 2 weeks.
Darifenacin: Dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision, confusion (older adults); anticholinergic burden is cumulative; avoid in narrow-angle glaucoma and urinary retention.
Darifenacin: Other anticholinergics add burden; cholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil) oppose the effect.
Mirabegron — Beta-3 adrenergic agonist
Mirabegron: Beta3 agonist: enhances detrusor relaxation during filling, with no anticholinergic activity.
Mirabegron: Overactive bladder (alone or with an antimuscarinic)
Mirabegron: Hypertension, nasopharyngitis, urinary tract infection, headache, urinary retention
Mirabegron: Severe uncontrolled hypertension, end-stage renal disease; caution with CYP2D6 substrates

Mirabegron: Formulation: ER tablets 25/50 mg; granules for suspension. Adult dose: 25 mg PO once daily, may increase to 50 mg after 4-8 weeks (maximum 25 mg with eGFR 15-29).
Mirabegron: Preferred in older adults or patients on other anticholinergics; may raise blood pressure; can combine with an antimuscarinic.
Mirabegron: Inhibits CYP2D6.
Tamsulosin — Alpha-1A selective blocker
Tamsulosin: Alpha1 blocker: relaxes bladder-neck, prostatic and proximal-urethral smooth muscle → better urinary flow in BPH; the same receptors set vascular tone.
Tamsulosin: Benign prostatic hyperplasia symptoms, ureteral stone passage (off-label)
Tamsulosin: Dizziness, orthostatic hypotension, retrograde ejaculation, rhinitis, intraoperative floppy iris syndrome
Tamsulosin: Hypersensitivity (sulfonamide allergy caution); strong CYP3A4 inhibitors
Tamsulosin: Toxicity/overdose: Orthostatic hypotension and syncope with first dose; floppy iris syndrome in cataract surgery
Tamsulosin: Formulation: Capsules 0.4 mg. Adult dose: 0.4 mg PO once daily 30 minutes after the same meal, may increase to 0.8 mg.
Tamsulosin: Uroselective — less vascular effect; still orthostasis, first-dose effect, floppy iris in cataract surgery.
Tamsulosin: Additive hypotension with antihypertensives and PDE5 inhibitors.
Silodosin — Highly uroselective alpha-1A blocker
Silodosin: Alpha1 blocker: relaxes bladder-neck, prostatic and proximal-urethral smooth muscle → better urinary flow in BPH; the same receptors set vascular tone.
Silodosin: Benign prostatic hyperplasia symptoms
Silodosin: Retrograde ejaculation (common), dizziness, orthostatic hypotension, diarrhea
Silodosin: Severe renal impairment (CrCl below 30 mL/min), severe hepatic impairment, strong CYP3A4 inhibitors
Silodosin: Toxicity/overdose: Orthostatic hypotension; floppy iris syndrome; contraindicated with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors
Silodosin: Formulation: Capsules 4/8 mg. Adult dose: 8 mg PO once daily with a meal (4 mg with moderate renal impairment).
Silodosin: Highly uroselective; avoid with CrCl below 30 mL/min.
Silodosin: Additive hypotension with antihypertensives and PDE5 inhibitors.
Doxazosin — Alpha-1 blocker (nonselective among alpha-1 subtypes)
Doxazosin: Alpha1 blocker: relaxes bladder-neck, prostatic and proximal-urethral smooth muscle → better urinary flow in BPH; the same receptors set vascular tone.
Doxazosin: Benign prostatic hyperplasia, hypertension
Doxazosin: Dizziness, orthostatic hypotension, first-dose syncope, fatigue, edema, floppy iris syndrome
Doxazosin: Hypersensitivity to quinazolines; caution with PDE5 inhibitors
Doxazosin: Toxicity/overdose: First-dose syncope and profound hypotension; restart at 1 mg after interruption of several days
Doxazosin: Formulation: Tablets 1/2/4/8 mg; ER tablets 4/8 mg. Adult dose: BPH: 1 mg PO daily at bedtime, titrate to 4-8 mg daily; hypertension: 1-16 mg daily.
Doxazosin: Less selective — lowers blood pressure more; first dose at bedtime (first-dose hypotension).
Doxazosin: Additive hypotension with antihypertensives and PDE5 inhibitors.
Terazosin — Alpha-1 blocker
Terazosin: Alpha1 blocker: relaxes bladder-neck, prostatic and proximal-urethral smooth muscle → better urinary flow in BPH; the same receptors set vascular tone.
Terazosin: Benign prostatic hyperplasia, hypertension
Terazosin: Dizziness, orthostatic hypotension, first-dose syncope, fatigue, peripheral edema, floppy iris syndrome
Terazosin: Hypersensitivity to quinazolines; caution with PDE5 inhibitors
Terazosin: Toxicity/overdose: First-dose hypotension and syncope; repeat titration after missed doses
Terazosin: Formulation: Tablets 1/2/5/10 mg; capsules. Adult dose: BPH: 1 mg PO at bedtime, titrate to 5-10 mg daily; hypertension: 1-5 mg daily (maximum 20 mg).
Terazosin: Less selective — lowers blood pressure more; first-dose effect.
Terazosin: Additive hypotension with antihypertensives and PDE5 inhibitors.

Sildenafil: PDE5 inhibitor: blocks cGMP breakdown, prolonging corpus cavernosum relaxation (needs sexual stimulation).

Sildenafil: Headache, flushing, dyspepsia, nasal congestion, visual changes (blue tint), hypotension
Sildenafil: Concurrent nitrates or riociguat, hypersensitivity; caution with alpha-1 blockers and severe cardiovascular disease
Sildenafil: Toxicity/overdose: Profound hypotension with nitrates; priapism over 4 hours is an emergency; sudden vision or hearing loss

Sildenafil: Absolute contraindication with any nitrate (or riociguat) — life-threatening hypotension; caution with alpha1 blockers; headache, flushing, dyspepsia.

Vardenafil: Erectile dysfunction
Vardenafil: Headache, flushing, rhinitis, dyspepsia, QT prolongation, visual changes
Vardenafil: Concurrent nitrates or riociguat, congenital long QT, class IA or III antiarrhythmics
Vardenafil: Toxicity/overdose: Profound hypotension with nitrates; QT prolongation; priapism
